paper.title: A self-adaptive tube restraint for free-energy calculations along path collective variables
paper.abstract: Path collective variables reduce a high-dimensional transition to a progress coordinate, s, and an orthogonal distance, z. Computing the free energy along s often requires restraining z, so that sampling embraces a tube centered on the reference path. However, a conventional fixed half-harmonic wall demands an a priori wall position that is both system dependent and s-dependent. Too tight a tube biases the path-projected free energy. Conversely, too loose a tube induces numerical instability and inter-channel leakage. We present an adaptive tube restraint, the wall position of which evolves on the fly to track a fixed contour ΔF∗ of the orthogonal free energy F(z∣s), widening automatically in flat basins and narrowing at pinched saddles, using a user-selected transverse energy scale. We prove that, for a locally harmonic perpendicular well, a contour-following tube captures an s-independent fraction of the orthogonal partition function, so that in the hard-wall limit, its bias cancels out. In stark contrast, the bias of a fixed-width tube varies with s and distorts the free-energy landscape. We probe the algorithm on several model potentials, on N-acetyl-N′-methylalanylamide isomerization, on the folding of the mini-protein chignolin, and on the folding-upon-binding of the ribose-binding protein. The method is implemented in the open-source Colvars library and is, therefore, usable within popular MD engines, such as NAMD, LAMMPS, GROMACS, and Tinker-HP.

paper.title: PolyNet: A Python Package for Polymer Informatics
paper.abstract: Polymers are used in a wide range of industries for diverse applications but formulating them to attain desired properties remains a challenging task. Polymer informatics has emerged as a powerful approach for the rational design of materials. Here, we present PolyNet, an open-source Python package that provides an end-to-end workflow for polymer informatics. PolyNet: 1) reads and validates datasets of polymer properties, including the monomer structures and their molar ratios; 2) creates vector- and graph-based representations of the polymers; 3) trains and optimises traditional machine learning (ML) models and graph neural networks (GNNs); 4) compares representations and models statistically; 5) deploys the models to screen in silico libraries of polymers, flagging polymers outside the applicability domain of the models and estimating their expected prediction error; and 6) interprets the models to understand structure–property relationships. PolyNet provides unique features such as: modelling of homopolymers and copolymers with any number of components, using the molar ratio of monomers in both vector- and graph-based representations; acceptance of textual representations of monomers or repeating units; calculation of polyBERT fingerprints and PolyMetriX and RDKit descriptors and fingerprints and accepting standalone user precalculated representations; benchmarking of all representation–model combinations on identical data splits using paired statistical tests; and chemically interpretable explanations through fragment-level attribution for GNNs and SHAP analysis for traditional ML models. Every experiment automatically records its configuration, data splits, hyperparameter search spaces and trained models, supporting full reproducibility in line with FAIR principles. PolyNet can be used through Python scripts, a command-line interface, or a graphical user interface for researchers without programming experience. We exemplify PolyNet by two case studies: glass transition temperature prediction for homopolymers, where cluster-based data splits showed that random splits overestimate model performance, the applicability domain identified less reliable predictions, and the model explanations recovered the known effect of chain mobility on T g ; and ¹⁹F MRI signal-to-noise ratio prediction for copolymers, where encoding monomer molar ratios is key to accurate predictions.

paper.title: Bridging molecular and nanometer scales in atmospheric new particle formation with quantum chemical modeling
paper.abstract: New particle formation (NPF) is important for our global climate and is assessed to contribute to up to half of the cloud condensation nuclei. However, there has been a knowledge gap in the size ranges that can be described accurately by quantum chemical methods and routinely measured by experimental techniques in the field. Based on quantum chemical calculations, boosted by machine learning (ML) techniques, we here present a novel framework for accurate modeling of the cluster formation dynamics directly from single molecules up to measurable nanoparticle sizes. Using sulfuric acid–base clustering as a proof-of-concept, we obtained temperaturedependent thermochemistry providing a consistent molecular description of nucleation and early growth up to approximately 2 nm, within the cluster-to-particle transition regime. The newly calculated data was used in the Atmospheric Cluster Dynamics Code (ACDC) to compare formation rates measured in CLOUD chamber, flow reactor experiments and in the field. Time-resolved simulations also allow direct comparison with 1.6 nm particle concentrations measured by a CPC FARM, in Pittsburgh, USA. This is the first time that the measured nanoparticles are explicitly modeled at molecular resolution without artificial splitting of “nucleation” and “growth”. Furthermore, instead of relying on nucleation potentials, the temporal evolution of chemical composition in FNPs can be tracked by timeseries simulation of actual nanoparticle concentrations. We couple our quantum chemical data to the aerosol transport and gas phase chemistry model (ADCHEM) and further demonstrate that we can reproduce trends of the nanoparticle concentrations observed in Hyltemossa, Sweden and verified the inconsistency caused by previous QC data, which contains only small clusters. The proposed methodology can be extended to other environments and mechanisms, provided that the necessary quantum chemical data are available or can be computed.

paper.title: Learnable coarsening for two-phase flow in porous media
paper.abstract: Abstract Hydrodynamic simulations of multi-phase flow in porous media are essential for oil production forecasting but require significant computational resources. Traditional approaches lead to high memory and time demands, restricting multi- scenario analysis. We propose a learnable coarsening algorithm based on graph neural networks (GNNs) with node aggregation for 2D two-phase flow modelling. The coarsened grid adapts to the reservoir geometry, its properties, and production data. Our algorithm is integrated with a graph-based finite volume method (FVM) solver, differentiable Voronoi tessellation, and a fully implicit upwind scheme. The unstructured computational grid is modeled as a graph with cell centers, adjacency edges, and rich a set of node features: coordinates, permeability, masks, distances to wells, permeability gradients, and wells influence potential. GNN produces soft assignments for probabilistic clustering, preserving wells and sensors. Training employs an FVM solver with physics-informed loss matching saturation and production rate time series at wells, promoting grid uniformity. Extending our prior works, our method enables coarsening by 10 times with relative error below 1%, accurately reproducing saturation fields, oil production, and water breakthrough on synthetic and realistic permeability fields

paper.title: Substituent Effects on the Photochemistry of Aqueous Phenolate-Based Anions Revealed by Extreme Ultraviolet Time-Resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy
paper.abstract: Phenolate (PhO-) is a prototypical chromophore and a recurring motif in photoactive biomolecular systems. Here, we use extreme-ultraviolet time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (XUV-TRPES) to probe how para-substitution redirects the photophysics of aqueous 4-nitrophenolate (4NP-) and 4-chlorophenolate (4CP-) anions. In 4NP-, following 400 nm excitation, internal charge reorganization accompanied by nitrogroup torsion forms a stabilized twisted intramolecular charge-transfer (TICT) configuration in 74 fs, efficiently funneling the population through a conical intersection to the ground state within 200 fs. Similar dynamics are seen upon excitation at 240 nm, although the initially excited state is even shorter-lived (40 fs). No hydrated electron production is seen at either wavelength. In 4CP-, following 240 nm excitation of the S2 state, internal conversion to S1 occurs within 120 fs. Chlorine substitution introduces a competing 1πσ* dissociative channel whose potential energy surface intersects S1, but the higher S1/1πσ* crossing barrier relative to 4BP- allows the S1 population to survive long enough (25 ps) for solvent-assisted electron ejection and internal conversion. The dynamics thus resemble those of PhO- rather than the sub-picosecond dissociative relaxation of 4BP-. Taken together with our previous PhO- and 4-bromophenolate (4BP-) measurements, these results reveal how para-substitution across this prototypical series drives the accessibility of competing excited-state dynamical processes, leading to very different photostability and photochemistry.

paper.title: Plasmonic Monolayer MoS 2 for Ultrathin Photoelectrodes in Neutral Water
paper.abstract: Photoelectrochemical (PEC) electrodes can be used to create hydrogen to sustainably generate low-cost fuel and produce petrochemical feedstock. However, most semiconductors that drive the aqueous redox reactions in PEC devices cannot survive in neutral water, critical for widescale commercial production. Emerging, two-dimensional monolayer semiconductors can be electrochemically stable but generally do not capture enough sunlight to produce effective amounts of hydrogen. In this work, we propose a new PEC architecture that uses plasmonic enhancement to increase photocurrent in a monolayer MoS 2 photocathode. By creating the first ZrN-based surface plasmon polariton (SPP) generator, we show fabricated nanostructures that plasmonically couple light with energies up to ~2.5 eV in water with near-100% light absorption. With transferred monolayer MoS 2 , the resulting Schottky diode demonstrates corrosion-free, fully stable photoactivity under 1-sun illumination in oxygenated, neutral water. We investigated and optimized the mechanisms of plasmonic enhancement, increasing photocurrent by up to 2.7x under AM1.5G illumination and 660% with wavelengths above the bandgap of monolayer MoS 2 . Furthermore, we show this architecture is compatible with standard roll-to-roll fabrication, and we use a technoeconomic analysis to estimate that levelized costs of hydrogen <$1/kg can be reasonably achieved with solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiencies of only 3.4%. Thus, with commercially scalable operational lifetimes and fabrication techniques, these results open the door to a new class of ultrathin PEC electrodes for economically feasible neutral water splitting applications.

paper.title: Computationally Guided Design of Facet-Defined Multielement Active Sites on Hexagonal Close-Packed High-Entropy-Alloy Nanosheets for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
paper.abstract: Abstract Nonconventional hexagonal close-packed (HCP) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide distinct catalytic surfaces, but their synthesis with well-defined facets remains challenging, leaving facet-dependent multielement ensemble effects largely unexplored. Here, we report the computationally guided realization of atomically thin RuRhIrPtPd HEA nanosheets with predominantly exposed HCP {001} facets for the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations identify HCP {001} as the most favorable facet over {100} and {110}, where near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption, narrow energy distribution, and balanced hydrogen/hydroxyl binding create an optimized alkaline HER landscape. Guided by this prediction, RuRhIrPtPd HEA atomic layers are epitaxially grown on HCP Ru nanosheets to maximize {001} exposure, with atomic-resolution electron microscopy and synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) confirming atomically mixed HEA layers. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the {001}-faceted HEA nanosheets exhibit higher alkaline HER activity and durability than irregular-faceted nanocrystal counterparts and commercial Pt/C. Climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations, operando XAS, and CO-stripping measurements identify Ru-centered ensembles as favorable Volmer sites, showing the lowest water-dissociation barrier of 1.04 eV compared with 1.13–1.47 eV for other metal sites, while neighboring multimetallic sites balance hydrogen and hydroxyl adsorption. This work provides a structural blueprint for harnessing facet-defined multielement ensembles to design high-entropy electrocatalysts.

paper.title: Transforming Unidirectional CO2 to CO Reduction Catalysis into a Bidirectional One via Rational Ligand Engineering
paper.abstract: Developing molecular catalysts capable of bidirectional CO2/CO conversion is crucial for advancing carbon‐neutral energy technologies, yet achieving such bidirectionality remains a formidable challenge. In recent years, several complexes, including [Co(II)(bpy)]2+, have been shown to catalyze the two-electron reduction of CO2 to CO selectively but not the reverse reaction of CO oxidation. One of the key features of metal complexes demonstrating bidirectionality (see e.g. ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 5934), is the access to a range of oxidation states. Since accessing high oxidation states for a Co centre is usually quite energy demanding, one alternative solution is to design ligands that can stabilize low oxidation states. Redox non-innocent ligands can stabilize formally very low oxidation states by storing the excess electrons on the ligands. Here, we present a cobalt complex bearing two redox‐non‐innocent bis(2‐(phenylazo)pyridine) (PAP) ligands that enables energy‐efficient, bidirectional CO2/CO electrocatalysis under mild conditions. Cooperative electron redistribution between the cobalt centre and the PAP ligand manifold facilitates multielectron storage and proton‐coupled electron transfer, allowing seamless switching between CO2 reduction and CO oxidation with minimal structural reorganisation. The catalyst displays a pronounced bias toward CO2 reduction, operating at an overpotential as low as 0.27 V with a turnover frequency of ~30 s-1 and Faradaic efficiency of 85%, while selectively oxidising CO back to CO2 with comparable activity. Spectroelectrochemical characterisation and multireference computational analysis reveal a mechanistic landscape governed by ligand‐centred redox flexibility and shared catalytic intermediates. This work introduces a rare example of a homogeneous, bidirectional cobalt catalyst, establishing a general design principle for next‐generation molecular systems that operate near thermodynamic potentials and close the carbon cycle through bidirectional electrocatalysis.

paper.title: Chemical Bonding Rules for Stacking-Sequence Stability in Bismuth Oxychloride Intergrowths and Their Consequences for Band Structure
paper.abstract: Abstract Metal oxyhalides are versatile materials, exhibiting properties relevant to photocatalysis, solid-state battery systems, ferromagnetism, multiferroics, and nonlinear optics. Here, mixed-metal oxyhalide intergrowths, layered materials formed by intercalating SrBi3O4Cl3 and Bi2GdO4Cl blocks along the c direction within a crystal, are reported. They are synthesized through a flux-based approach in which the SrBi3O4Cl3-to-Bi2GdO4Cl ratio can be precisely controlled. Despite the structural and compositional flexibility of such intergrowths, there is no general framework for predicting which local structural arrangements are preferred. Density functional theory combined with Bader charge analysis shows that preferred stacking sequences are those that minimize charge disproportionation across distinct chlorine environments, consistent with Pauling’s fifth rule, and we support this bonding-based framework through computational cation substitution that shifts the ionic-covalent balance of the metal–chloride bonding. With the preferred stacking arrangement established, this same system further reveals that intergrowth layering and Sr/Bi site occupancy modulate the interaction between the Bi3+ lone pair and anion p orbitals. Density functional theory calculations reveal that intergrowth formation destabilizes the O-2p orbitals, raising the valence band maximum for visible-light absorption, with the lone-pair interaction and layering-driven internal electrostatic field acting as competing effects on the resulting band gap. Significantly, this experimental-computational study establishes a transferable, bonding-based framework for stacking-sequence stability in layered oxyhalide intergrowths, while also clarifying how the same structural levers used to control stability can be tuned to engineer band structure.

paper.title: Linear inductive bias boosts extrapolative molecular discovery by Bayesian active learning in the small-data limit
paper.abstract: Bayesian active learning is widely used for molecular discovery, yet surrogate selection remains challenging when scarce initial data must guide the search beyond the observed property range. Here we benchmark diverse Gaussian process (GP) configurations across ten small-molecule and polymer datasets, focusing on the extrapolative regime where the initial labeled samples are drawn exclusively from below the median of the target property distribution. We identify explicit linear structure as an effective inductive bias for data-scarce extrapolative discovery: linear-kernel GPs provide a strong baseline, while adding linear components to a stationary kernel helps mitigate poor outcomes in the tail of the performance distribution. However, this advantage weakens under later-stage interpolative regime, where adaptive surrogate selection can further improve the discovery performance. These findings support incorporating linear inductive biases into data-driven materials discovery, where data scarcity and limited coverage of the design space are the norm rather than the exception.

paper.title: Simulating Catalytic Resonance with Molecular Dynamics
paper.abstract: Static heterogeneous catalysts are constrained by the Sabatier principle, where their overall turnover is limited by balancing the kinetics of reactant binding, surface reaction, and product unbinding. Modulating the surface binding energies between a strong binding state and a weak binding state can overcome this limit. For such a dynamic catalyst, a maximum turnover is achieved at a catalytic resonance modulating frequency. Here we demonstrate that classical molecular simulation approaches can be used to study this phenomena. Our method introduces a generic classical model for a surface reaction with time-dependent surface binding energy. Using a non-equilibrium molecular simulation in which reactants tend to be added to the system and products tend to be removed, we can simulate many catalyst cycles. Our approach reproduces catalytic resonance, with the dynamic catalyst providing up to a three-order-of-magnitude boost in turnover compared to the static catalyst. We further demonstrate the presence of a second resonant frequency in the gas phase, associated with resonance of the reacting bond. The general approach outlined here can be extended to more detailed models and used to study the molecular-scale effects of surface modulation and to computationally test input frequency, amplitude, and waveform for programmable catalysts.

paper.title: Light-assisted bifunctionality in CuPt single-atom alloys for propane dehydroaromatization
paper.abstract: Dilute plasmonic alloys offer a route to couple light harvesting with site-specific surface chemistry, but how host and dopant sites cooperate during multi-step hydrocarbon transformations remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that silica-supported CuPt single-atom alloys decouple the elementary steps of propane dehydroaromatization. The Cu host promotes visible light-assisted C-C coupling of C3 intermediates, but Cu remains inactive for direct alkane C-H activation. Introducing atomically dispersed Pt in Cu unlocks propane dehydrogenation and enables a parallel aromatization pathway to benzene under illumination. Isotopic labeling, wavelength- and power-dependent kinetics, catalyst comparisons, and theoretical modeling support a bifunctional mechanism in which Pt sites generate dehydrogenated C3 intermediates, the Cu host facilitates C-C coupling, and the Cu-Pt interface promotes cyclization. These results establish light-assisted single-atom/host cooperation as a design principle for plasmonic alkane upgrading.

paper.title: Turning Up the Heat: Investigation into the Driving Forces of the Hofmeister Effect in Water Vibrational Spectra
paper.abstract: The Hofmeister series has historically been used to rank ions according to their impact on the solubility of proteins in aqueous solutions. Strongly hydrating salts, which stabilize the native structure of proteins, leading to their “salting-out,” are referred to as kosmotropes (“structure-makers”). Weakly hydrating salts, which facilitate protein denaturing and “salting-in,” are referred to as chaotropes (“structure-breakers”). While the Hofmeister effect has been extensively studied, the underlying thermodynamic driving forces are not well understood. Recent fluctuation theory calculations have suggested that the Hofmeister effect observed in the infrared (IR) spectrum of aqueous alkali–halide solutions is predominantly entropically driven. Here, experimental support for this hypothesis is provided through temperature-dependent Fourier transform IR (FTIR) spectroscopy. The FTIR OH stretch spectrum of alkali halides dissolved in isotopically dilute HOD/D2O was collected and the temperature derivative of the lineshape was used to extract relevant thermodynamic potentials. It was observed that while the effective enthalpy is nearly ion-independent, a reduction of the entropic cost to form stronger hydrogen-bonds (H-bonds) scales with decreasing halide size, suggesting that this contribution is the driving force for this observed Hofmeister effect.

paper.title: Structural Resolution in Feature Attribution Analysis of Molecular Graph Neural Networks
paper.abstract: Machine learning models based on molecular graphs can evaluate the contribution of each atom to a prediction using feature attribution methods. However, in chemistry, molecular properties are frequently discussed in terms of both individual atoms and structural units comprising multiple atoms, e.g., functional groups and substituents. In this study, we defined the granularity of the structural units used to present and evaluate feature attributions as their structural resolution, and we investigated how the relationship between feature attributions obtained from different molecular graph models varied with structural resolution. These attributions were evaluated at two structural resolutions, i.e., individual atoms and chemically defined structural groups. The group-level feature attributions exhibited higher intermodel agreement than the corresponding atom-level attributions for every target property and model pair. These results indicate that although the allocation of contributions to individual atoms can vary depending on the model architecture, the contribution patterns shared across multiple models can be retained at the level of entire structural groups.

paper.title: Iridium-Ruthenium Oxide for the Oxygen Evolution Reaction: Correlation between Calcination Temperature–Morphology–Activity Interplay
paper.abstract: Abstract A key challenge in water electrolysis is establishing structure–activity relationships to understand and improve IrRuOx-based catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in a PEM water electrolyser. We report a simple, scalable modified Adams fusion method for preparing highly OER-active IrRuOx with various sizes and shapes. This practical approach enables investigation of how heat treatment affects particle size, morphology, and the nature of surface species, and how these factors influence the OER activity of IrRuOx. P-XRD, HR-TEM/SEM-EDS, and TGA/DSC studies indicate a transition from an amorphous hydrated oxide (IrRuOx@350) to a crystalline hydrated phase (IrRuOx@400°C, IrRuOx@450°C, IrRuOx@500°C, and IrRuOx@520°C), with surface species strongly linked to OER activity. IrRuOx synthesized at 500°C, consisting of 22.22 nm particles with an electrochemical surface area of 903 cm 2 , shows the highest OER activity in 0.5 M H 2 SO 4 (E = 220 mV and a Tafel slope of 24.41 mV/dec at 10 mA/cm 2 ). In contrast, amorphous IrRuOx synthesized at 350°C shows better stability at a potential of 1.27 V. A variation in intrinsic OER activity was associated with the predominant termination of rod-shaped particles by highly ordered (110) and (200) facets. These results highlight the important role of calcination temperature in achieving the best balance between activity and durability of materials towards OER in PEMWE applications.

paper.title: Semiempirical Quantum Chemistry in the Age of ab initio Data and Differentiable Programming: II. Parameter Optimization
paper.abstract: Semiempirical quantum chemistry (SQC) represents an invaluable asset in the toolbox of molecular and materials modeling. Thanks to their explicit quantum-mechanical treatment of electrons, they allow to capture an array of local and non-local interaction mechanisms and offers access to electronic structure properties, which can be of crucial importance in order to better understand and design molecular systems and materials. In a previous publication, we presented our recent advances within the PySEQM package, enabling rapid gradient evaluations for SQC parameters and thus developing an efficient and reliable back-end for SQC parametrizations. In this work, we detail our implementation of this parametrization procedure, SQCFit, and its features. Offering a high degree of automation, SQCFit implements a suite of tailor-made tools for the optimization of SQC parameters. Specifically, we present local versus global parametrization schemes, the use of train-validation splits and early stopping to avoid overfitting, and advanced scoring/loss functions including appropriately standardized quantitative error measures as well as more qualitative measures such as the performance in ranking candidate systems according to a given molecular property. Based on a set of test applications, we highlight how SQCFit allows to obtain performant parametrizations tailor-made for the modern use cases of SQC.

paper.title: Machine Learning the Nonradiative Decay Modes in Photochemical Processes
paper.abstract: Abstract Nonradiative decay in photoexcited molecular systems is driven by nuclear motion toward conical intersections (CIs), where electronic states become degenerate and nonadiabatic transitions occur. Identifying the nuclear degrees of freedom responsible for CI access from nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD) simulations remains challenging, because the underlying motions are high-dimensional and collective. Here, we introduce an unsupervised, information-theoretic framework based on differentiable information imbalance (DII) to identify the nuclear coordinates governing CI access directly from trajectory surface hopping (TSH) simulations. By quantifying correlations between structural descriptors and electronic observables, including energy gaps and oscillator strengths, the method ranks nuclear degrees of freedom by their predictive relevance. A multistep protocol then extracts low-dimensional, physically interpretable modes associated with nonradiative decay. We apply the framework to the methaniminium cation, furan, l-glutamine, l-pyroglutamine ammonium, and a photoactive molecular motor. Across all systems, the method recovers known mechanistic coordinates while revealing the relative importance of competing modes when multiple structural distortions contribute to the CI access. The analysis also reveals a systematic distinction between observables: energy gaps are typically governed by a small number of localized coordinates, whereas oscillator strengths depend on more-extended and distributed structural rearrangements. Overall, the DII-based framework combines predictive power with direct interpretability, providing a general and scalable route for extracting mechanistic insights from high-dimensional NAMD data and constructing reduced-dimensional models of excited-state dynamics.

paper.title: Metal Fluorides: All-In-One Supports for Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ammonia Synthesis
paper.abstract: Abstract Ammonia, an emerging energy carrier, demands advanced catalysts for synthesis under mild conditions to integrate with green hydrogen. We herein establish a family of metal fluoride supports (MFn, M = Li, Na, K, Mg, Ca, or Ba) as a tunable “all-in-one” platform for ruthenium (Ru) catalysts. These Ru/MFn systems unify the critical merits of various existing catalysts, such as support-mediated activation of reactants and air stability. Varying the host cation can direct the catalytic pathway. Consequently, Ru/NaF exhibits excellent turnover frequency, while Ru/BaF2 delivers an NH3 synthesis rate of 58.0 mmolNH3 gcat–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 0.9 MPa─surpassing all reported Ru-based catalysts with ≤4 wt % Ru and without external promoters. Advanced characterization reveals that the fluorine vacancy formation energies of the alkali and alkaline-earth lattices, together with the vacancy-reactant interactions, dictate the divergent catalytic mechanisms mediated by different active sites. This work expands the chemistry of metal fluorides, launching a new paradigm for potentially viable NH3-synthesis under mild conditions.

paper.title: A chiral superlattice route to spin-split topological antiferromagnetism
paper.abstract: Chirality has emerged as a new mechanism for inducing spin and Berry-curvature phenomena in quantum materials and molecular chemistry1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Collinear antiferromagnets (AFMs) are promising for spintronics and topological magnetism, yet realizing large Berry curvature and spin-split bands remains challenging8,9. Here we report a chiral-superlattice route to spin-split topological phenomena from collinear antiferromagnetism. We study the collinear AFM UOTe, in which we show a spontaneous chiral superlattice arising from frozen chiral phonons at a finite wave vector. Without the superlattice, the pristine collinear AFM in UOTe has neither Berry curvature nor spin-split bands. When electrons move through the chiral superlattice, their orbital Bloch wavefunction and quantum geometry are modulated by the strong chiral superlattice potential, generating large Berry curvature, which we detect by the nonlinear Hall effect. At 150 K, the chiral-superlattice-induced Berry curvature couples to the collinear AFM order, leading to an anomalous Hall angle of about 0.14 abruptly near the Néel temperature TN which is among the largest in bulk magnets. Moreover, our spin Hanle precession measurement shows that the chiral superlattice also generates spin-polarized current from the collinear AFM, a long-standing goal in spintronics. We shed light on the supermodulation formation mechanism based on chemical ion size and physical interlayer–intralayer energy competitions, which we use to propose a design principle to discover similar bond-mismatch superlattices, providing a chiral superlattice pathway through real-space engineering of quantum geometry10,11.

paper.title: Claudin-2 protects from enteropathogenic E. coli-infection and colitis by promoting crypt fetalization via β1-integrin/FAK/YAP signaling
paper.abstract: Abstract Citrobacter rodentium ( Cra ) infection, a murine model of enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) infection, induces crypt proliferation that potentially promotes mucosal healing and pathogen clearance, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Cra infection upregulates claudin-2 (CLDN2), which has been proposed to facilitate pathogen clearance by enhancing Na⁺ flux and diarrhea. However, CLDN2 is dispensable for intestinal Na⁺ homeostasis. Here, we investigate whether Cra -induced CLDN2 protects against Cra -infection and colitis by regulating crypt proliferation. Using mice with intestinal epithelial-specific CLDN2 overexpression or deletion ( Cldn2 KO), we evaluate the role of CLDN2 in Cra colonization, inflammation, and epithelial regeneration. Organoid cultures assess epithelial-intrinsic mechanisms, while co-immunoprecipitation identifies CLDN2-associated signaling complexes. CLDN2 overexpression protects against Cra colonization and colitis, whereas Cldn2 KO mice exhibit increased bacterial burden, exacerbated inflammation, and impaired crypt proliferation. Mechanistically, CLDN2 promotes crypt fetal-like reprogramming (fetalization), which is suppressed in Cldn2 KO mice. Inhibiting EGFR-activation abolishes CLDN2 induction and phenocopies Cldn2 KO phenotype. Furthermore, CLDN2 promotes FAK and YAP activation by stabilizing the β1-integrin-FAK complex, thereby driving crypt fetalization. Collectively, these findings identify CLDN2 as a critical regulator of mucosal defense and epithelial regeneration through activation of the β1-integrin-FAK-YAP signaling axis, beyond its classical role in paracellular ion permeability.

paper.title: Block-fitness modeling of the global air mobility network
paper.abstract: Abstract Accurate representations of origin-destination (OD) passenger flows on the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, OD data are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model that treats air mobility as a stochastic process within a sparse maximum-entropy framework, informed by aggregate traffic volumes of individual locations and geographic regions. The model accurately reconstructs both network structure and mobility flows, yielding epidemic spreading trajectories that closely match those obtained using real mobility data. Furthermore, the method can be effectively implemented using open data on flight routes and airport traffic, reducing dependence on proprietary datasets. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for scenario analysis and policy design in global mobility systems.

paper.title: Why Interfacial Electric Fields May Appear Weaker: An Electron-Density-Based Study of the Flat Air–Water Interface
paper.abstract: Abstract The catalytic properties of water microdroplets are often attributed to strong interfacial electric fields, yet the nature of these fields remains debated. Here we combine quantum data-driven many-body molecular dynamics, ab initio resampling, and spatially resolved electric field evaluations to rigorously assess intermolecular electrostatics at the flat air–water interface. The calculated local intermolecular quantity may be viewed as a microsolvation electric-field descriptor of the environment experienced by a molecular species approaching or residing near the interface. By classifying molecules using two complementary interface definitions and going beyond classical partial-charge methods, we obtain field maps directly from the electronic charge density. Similarly to recent experimental findings, the bulk and interfacial field distributions overlap strongly, while their mean values exhibit a modest interfacial reduction of ∼10%. Correlations with the density profiles obtained from different reference frames indicate that density depletion near the surface contributes to this attenuation. Beyond offering an electron-density-based methodology for evaluating local electric fields, these findings suggest that exceptionally strong local fields alone may not fully account for the enhanced reactivity reported in microdroplets.

paper.title: Quantum-Entangled Four-Proton Waltz of Anomalous Transport in Water Hydrogen Bond Network
paper.abstract: Proton transfer mechanism along water hydrogen bond network lies in the fundamental question in chemical dynamics. The mechanism remains challenge due to nuclear quantization and many-body correlation. We develop a quantum dynamical model framework that treats electrons and multiple transferring protons on equal footing, and integrate it with isotope measurement by scanning tunneling microscopy of a surface‑bound water tetramer. The simulations reveal the importance of quantum correlation among stepwise electron–proton intermediate states, which quantum coherently drives a synchronized, concerted four‑proton switch between two chiral hydrogen‑bond configurations. Populations periodically decay from one chiral arrangement and reappear in the other, whose oscillation amplitude is strongly suppressed by modest symmetry breaking from isotopic substitution. This mechanism accounts for an anomalous isotope trend experimentally in which the low‑symmetry, singly deuterated tetramer (H2O)3(D2O) switches as slowly as the high‑symmetry, fully deuterated (D2O)4 that eludes semiclassical tunneling kinetics. The framework establishes a practical route to study multi-proton quantum correlation in hydrogen-bond networks on surfaces.

paper.title: The Manifestation of the Electrochemical Potential Gradient in the Kinetic Landscapes of Interfacial Electrochemistry
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The electrochemical potential gradient constitutes a free energy driving force. Understanding how this gradient manifests itself and drives electronic and ionic charges through the bulk and across interfaces is important across the natural sciences, including in solar cells, batteries, heterogeneous and biocatalysis, and proton pumps and motors. Despite this, literature often misrepresents the electrochemical potential gradient. In the extreme, it is simply replaced by an electric field as an apparent driving force. Here, we use energy band diagrams to review the basics of electrochemical charge separation and to inform on the nonequilibrium boundary conditions in interfacial electrochemistry. We explain that the thermodynamic driving force along the reaction coordinate needs to be distinguished from chemical potential changes in the extended environment that can modulate activation barriers, without necessarily being a driving force themselves. To this end, we focus on the role of overpotential‐dependent excess charge and electric fields, before discussing overpotential‐dependent coverages and multistep reactions. We close by explaining how these local chemical potential changes give rise to a multidimensional kinetic landscape that cannot be compressed into single‐descriptor kinetics.

paper.title: Electric fields control static charge during contact-friction-separation
paper.abstract: Abstract Contact electrification occurs when two materials rub against one another. This is either a problem, such as when charge builds up during powder processing, or an exploited phenomenon to harvest energy, as is the case in triboelectric nanogenerators. However, why contact electrification occurs remains a topic of hot debate, with ions, adsorbates, electrons and combinations thereof being ascribed the charge carriers. Irrespective of the charge carrier however, there must be a driving force inducing charge to separate and move from one surface to another. Herein, we demonstrate that electric fields, either applied externally or spontaneously generated at an interface can completely alter and even invert surface charge measured after contact electrification in polymer-polymer contact. Applying an external electric field allows the direct control of both magnitude and polarity static charge on dielectric polymers. These results are coupled to simulations that show the applied electric field is on the order of the fields generated by the flexoelectric effect – providing prima facie evidence of flexoelectric driven contact electrification.

paper.title: “Direct Injection” Bubble Growth Mediated by Nano‐Interfaced Electrodes for Efficient Chlorine Production
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The chlor‐alkali industry, with the chlorine evolution reaction (CER) as its core anodic process, accounts for nearly 4% of global electricity consumption. The development of energy‐efficient and stable CER system is therefore urgently needed. Nano‐interfaced electrodes exhibit superior catalytic performance, yet their mechanism for energy saving and system stability remains incompletely understood. Here, we combine a high‐speed camera and confocal laser scanning microscope Platform to visualize and digitalize the bubble evolution and the bubble‐induced overpotential ( ƞ bub ). We provide direct visual evidence that the bubble‐induced concentration gradients and fluid flow field disturbances are key regulators of overpotential, and that the nano‐interfaced electrode exhibits an ƞ bub of only approximately 49% of that of the flat‐interfaced electrode. Specifically, the nano interface not only generates a stronger interfacial electric field and enhanced bubble‐induced interfacial turbulence—which promote the Cl − migration to the electrode surface—but also induces a “direct‐injection” mode of bubble growth that mitigates the accumulation of reaction products near the electrode. Moreover, the Cl − enrichment capacity of the nano interface endows the near‐interface solution with ionic buffering capability, effectively suppressing potential fluctuations. This work demonstrates that regulating bubble dynamics is key to constructing energy‐saving and stable gas‐evolving electrochemical systems.

paper.title: Field‐Effect Induced Interfacial Water Restructuring Accelerates Zinc‐Catalyzed Hydrodeoxygenation
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The deoxygenation of biomass‐derived molecules is thermodynamically challenging yet essential for their conversion to commodity chemicals. Metallic zinc is a promising material for deoxygenation due to its strong reductive properties, but sluggish kinetics and harsh reaction conditions detract from practical application. Here, we hypothesize that zinc‐catalyzed hydrodeoxygenation could be limited by inefficient proton transport due to disordered interfacial water structure. Using the transformation of dihydroxyacetone to acetone as a model reaction, we identified the rate‐determining step to be an Eley–Rideal‐type proton‐coupled electron transfer from water to the hydroxyacetone intermediate. Applying an electric field accelerates this step by restructuring the interfacial hydrogen‐bond network and promoting direct proton transfer, thereby enabling a 10 3 ‐fold increase in surface‐area‐normalized turnover frequency and Faradaic efficiencies of 63%–70% at current densities up to 300 mA/cm 2 . These findings highlight interfacial water restructuring as a powerful lever for enhancing hydrodeoxygenation efficiency.

paper.title: Hydroxyl-terminated carbosilane dendrimer films at water–toluene and water–air interfaces
paper.abstract: We report a fully atomistic molecular dynamics study of fourth-generation amphiphilic carbosilane dendrimers adsorbed at water–toluene and water–air interfaces across a wide range of surface densities. The dendrimers, featuring a tetrafunctional silicon core, trifunctional =Si(CH3)– branching units, and terminal hydroxyl groups, adopt a characteristic “umbrella” conformation at low coverage, with hydrophilic termini anchored in water and the hydrophobic core aligned with the nonpolar phase. Interfacial chemistry fundamentally modulates this architecture: favorable toluene–core interactions promote core swelling and homogeneous lateral dispersion, whereas the sharp hydrophobic mismatch at the water–air interface drives dendrimer aggregation. Lateral compression induces a systematic transition from flattened, anisotropic conformations to more isotropic, near-spherical geometries, accompanied by redistribution of hydrogen bonds from dendrimer–water to intra- and interdendrimer contacts. Under strong confinement, steric crowding and transient interdendrimer hydrogen bonding lead to dynamic arrest, with lateral diffusion suppressed by orders of magnitude. These findings establish a unified molecular picture of how surface density and solvent compatibility jointly control conformation, interactions, and mobility in amphiphilic dendrimer monolayers, providing design principles for tunable interfacial materials with tailored mechanical and transport properties.

paper.title: The pH effect in hydrogen evolution is a consequence of creating a solvated hydroxide ion
paper.abstract: The hydrogen evolution reaction is orders of magnitude faster in acid than in base on the same electrode, a pH effect that first-principles calculations have not quantitatively reproduced. We trace this failure to the treatment of the ions: standard density functionals with standard solvation treatments undersolvate hydroxide–the ionic product of alkaline hydrogen evolution–by more than 1 eV against experiment and coupled cluster benchmarks, an error that tracks the functional’s self-interaction error. A screened hybrid functional with reduced self-interaction error yields Au(111) Volmer barriers whose acidalkaline difference falls within the measured range of onset-potential separations, whereas semi-local functionals predict zero to three times the measured value. Quantitative computational electrocatalysis therefore demands functionals benchmarked jointly against ion solvation thermochemistry and molecule-surface energetics.

paper.title: Restructuring hydrogen-bonding networks via hydroxyl-functionalized covalent organic frameworks for efficient nitrate electroreduction
paper.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR) is a promising strategy for nitrate removal and ammonia synthesis, but its efficiency is largely limited by sluggish proton transfer kinetics and poor reaction selectivity. Herein, we rationally design a series of hydroxyl-functionalized copper phthalocyanine-based covalent organic frameworks (Cu-COF-nOH) to regulate interfacial proton transfer via restructuring hydrogen-bonding networks. The hydroxyl functional groups in Cu-COF-nOH enhance water adsorption and dissociation to enrich interfacial proton supply. Optimized hydroxyl loading further induces the formation of continuous hydrogen-bond chains, enabling oriented and accelerated proton shuttling toward Cu active centers instead of stochastic diffusion. Electrocatalytic tests in 0.5 M nitrate electrolyte show that the optimal Cu-COF-4OH catalyst achieves an ammonia Faradaic efficiency of 93.20% and an NH 3 yield rate of 65.84 mg·h −1 , along with excellent long-term stability, outperforming most state-of-the-art NO 3 RR electrocatalysts. Combined with in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations, we clearly clarify that hydroxyl-mediated hydrogen-bonding restructuring plays a critical role in boosting proton transfer kinetics and reaction selectivity. This work provides a versatile interface engineering strategy for efficient multiproton/electron-coupled electrocatalytic reactions, offering insights into the design of high-performance NO 3 RR catalysts.

paper.title: Residue Protonation States Shape the Photodynamics of Red Fluorescent Proteins
paper.abstract: Understanding the protonation equilibria of key residues in fluorescent proteins, particularly those buried and involved in hydrogen bonding with the chromophore, is crucial for modeling their photodynamical behavior. Using mCherry as a model system, we investigate the protonation effects of two ionizable residues, GLU 215 and LYS 70, located within 4 Å of the chromophore, on the protein's photodynamics. Although GLU and LYS should be fully deprotonated and protonated respectively at pH=7.5 and 300K in water, constant pH molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the fractions of protonated GLU 215 and LYS 70 are both near 50% in mCherry at pH=7.5 and 300K. These co-existing protonation microstates modulate chromophore geometry and hydrogen bonding patterns on the ground state, affecting the accessibility of different non-radiative decay pathways on the first singlet excited state (S1). Upon deprotonation of GLU 215 and loss of its hydrogen bond with the chromophore, the protein environment both sterically restricts chromophore twisting and removes the electrostatic driving force for this motion on S1. These findings provide valuable insights for designing brighter red fluorescent proteins by selective stabilization of residue protonation states that block non-radiative decay pathways.

paper.title: Improved desalination by polymer grafting
paper.abstract: Freshwater scarcity demands desalination technologies that are efficient, scalable, and sustainable. Capacitive deionisation (CDI) is promising but remains limited by inefficient ion adsorption and poor charge utilisation. Here, we show that suitably chosen polyampholytic block copolymer grafting can substantially enhance CDI performance, via a combination of dipolar response and steric effects. Using mean-field classical density functional theory and grand-canonical Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that such polymer grafted electrodes enable strongly improved desalination performance, without altering the pore architecture. Even an electrode grafting by simple neutral polymers can generate an improvement, although a suitably designed block polymer architecture offers an additional performance gain. These results establish interfacial block copolymer grafting as a powerful route toward high-performance, membrane-free desalination.

paper.title: Potential‐Gated Spin Crossover Triggers Fe─N─C Catalyst Demetallation
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Atomically dispersed Fe─N─C catalysts are leading candidates for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), yet their rapid demetallation in acidic media remains a critical bottleneck for commercial fuel cell viability. While nitrogen protonation is known to correlate with demetallation, the fundamental electronic and structural triggers—specifically the role of Fe redox and spin‐state transitions at the ∼0.8 V dissolution onset—remain poorly understood. Here, using constant‐potential ab initio molecular dynamics (CP‐AIMD), we uncover a potential‐gated spin crossover mechanism that triggers O 2 ‐independent demetallation in acidic electrolytes. Near 0.8 V, reduction from Fe(III) to Fe(II) is coupled to an intermediate‐spin‐to‐high‐spin crossover that promotes pseudo‐Jahn–Teller out‐of‐plane distortion and dynamic formation of a hydrated FeN 4– 2H 2 O* precursor. The resulting Fe─N bond elongation increases the thermodynamic susceptibility of adjacent N sites to protonation, leading to rapid Fe─N bond cleavage and Fe detachment in acidic electrolyte. Simulated x‐ray absorption spectra derived from this mechanism closely reproduce experimental spectroscopic signatures of potential‐dependent Fe dissolution. These results identify a possible electronic and structural basis for protonation‐assisted Fe loss and motivate testing spin‐state and ligand‐field control as strategies for improving the stability of pyridinic FeN 4 sites.

paper.title: Nonadiabatic Semiclassical Polariton Dynamics: Excited State Proton Transfer of Aminopropenal
paper.abstract: The interplay between strong light-matter coupling and nonadiabatic molecular dynamics provides a promising route to control chemical reactivity. Here, we develop a framework for simulating polaritonic chemistry with on-the-fly semiclassical nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, employing the linearized semiclassical initial value representation. With this approach, we simulate the nonadiabatic molecular dynamics under strong light-matter coupling, presenting results for excited state proton transfer of aminopropenal. Light-matter interactions are described using a Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian formulated in the adiabatic electronic basis, where the electronic energies, transition moments, and nuclear forces are evaluated on the fly. We characterize how light-matter coupling reshapes reaction pathways and redistributes photonic and electronic character of individual states along the trajectory, finding that photonic character of the lower polaritonic state decreases in time as the molecular geometry relaxes, demonstrating that the cavity effect is strongest during the initial dynamics. We find that for aminopropenal, the main effect of cavity coupling on the dynamics is not altering the proton transfer barrier, but instead altering the excited-state relaxation network by introducing an additional polaritonic state with favorable proton transfer energetics. By analyzing the population transfer between excited states, we find that cavity coupling leads to population being temporarily redirected into this intermediate state, delaying population relaxation to a high-barrier excited state. This change in timing results in a higher fraction of trajectories undergoing proton transfer. Our new computational protocol that connects on-the-fly semiclassical nonadiabatic dynamics and polaritonic frameworks provides trajectory-resolved insight into how cavity coupling modifies nonadiabatic population transfer and proton-transfer dynamics.

paper.title: Heteroatom Engineering Enables Oxygen-Tolerant Electrochemical Direct Air Capture
paper.abstract: Electrochemical direct CO2 capture using redox-active carriers offers an alternative to thermal amine scrubbing but requires molecules that combine strong CO2 binding with tolerance toward oxygen and water. Here, we show that incorporating pyridinic nitrogen into an ortho-quinone framework provides this combination in 1,10phenanthroline-5,6-dione (PD). Comparison of PD with phenanthrenequinone (PQ) and the analogue 1,10phenanthroline (PT) isolates the role of pyridinic nitrogen in tuning the redox potential and CO2 capture behaviour of the quinone core. Electrochemical measurements, density functional theory (DFT), in situ FT-IR, and 13C NMR spectroscopy support strong and reversible CO2 binding through the electrochemically reduced dianion (log𝐾 = 9.8). The capture chemistry established in homogeneous electrolyte was subsequently translated to PD immobilised on a carbon-felt electrode and demonstrated in a near-neutral aqueous electrolyte. Under a 9.3% CO2 feed, the PD-modified electrode sustained reversible CO2 capture and release over 16 h with an electron-utilisation efficiency of 96% and a minimum energy requirement of 44-56 kJ mol-1 CO2. Isotope-sensitive in situ FT-IR measurements and the pH response during aqueous cycling further support cation participation in charge compensation. These results establish heteroatom engineering as a molecular design strategy for developing oxygen- and water-tolerant quinone redox carriers and provide a pathway toward electrochemical CO2 capture from dilute emission streams.

paper.title: Crystallography‐Dependent Plating/Stripping Kinetics and Interfacial Morphologies in Zn Metal Anodes
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Crystallographic orientation governs Zn deposition, dissolution, and cycling stability, but its influence on interfacial charge‐transfer kinetics remains difficult to quantify. Here, scanning electrochemical cell microscopy coupled with fast scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) is used to resolve Zn plating and stripping on single‐crystal (002), (100), and (101) surfaces. Meniscus‐confined measurements reveal facet‐dependent branch‐specific apparent zero‐current potentials and apparent exchange current densities, j 0 , with the kinetic ordering j 0 (100) > j 0 (101) > j 0 (002) for both plating and stripping. This ordering is reproduced across independently prepared electrodes and retained over different scan rates and aqueous electrolytes. Beyond charge transfer, Zn removal and regrowth are strongly crystallographically encoded: dissolution footprints preserve the symmetry of the parent facets, while potentiostatically deposited Zn adopts substrate‐dependent growth geometries. These coupled kinetic and morphological differences translate directly to battery performance. Despite its slower apparent kinetics, the close‐packed, low‐energy (002) facet exhibits the longest cycling life in Zn/Zn symmetric cells and substantially improved capacity retention in both polyaniline/Zn and Na 0.33 V 2 O 5 /Zn full cells, whereas the faster (100) and (101) interfaces fail earlier. These findings establish a facet‐dependent kinetics–stability trade‐off and show that durable Zn anodes require coordinated control of charge transfer, dissolution topology, and crystallographic reconstruction.

paper.title: Structural Fluctuation in Liquids Revealed by High-Order Harmonic Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract High-order harmonic generation (HHG) in liquids has attracted considerable attention, yet the fundamental processes responsible for the liquid-related differences are still not well elucidated. Here we systematically investigate the liquid-HHG spectra of water, acetonitrile, methanol, ethanol, and 1- and 2-propanols. Within the framework of the three-step recollision model, we extract the values of maximum excursion length (Lmax) of the electron prior to its recapture. We establish a phenomenological scaling law linking the experimental Lmax values to the liquid properties (viscosity, mass density, and molecular thermal speed), exhibiting an intrinsic connection between the HHG spectra and structural fluctuations within liquids. This relationship is further validated through a quantitative comparison of the macroscopic self-diffusion coefficients of the liquids. Our findings also indicate that HHG spectroscopy emerges as a promising tool for probing liquid properties.

paper.title: Unilateral Functionalization of Covalent Organic Frameworks: Local Electronic Modulation and Morphology-Enabled Mass Transport for Electrocatalytic Hydrogen Peroxide Production
paper.abstract: Abstract Achieving high selectivity and activity in the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e– ORR) pathway critically depends on the synergistic modulation of a catalyst’s electronic structure and mass diffusion channels. This work proposes an asymmetric modulation strategy via unilateral functionalization, in which −CH3, −CN, −SO3H, and −NO2 moieties are incorporated into a series of covalent organic frameworks (COFs), systematically unraveling the multilevel regulatory mechanisms exerted by functional groups from molecular to macroscopic morphological scales. The research demonstrates that introducing strong electron-withdrawing −NO2 groups can effectively enhance charge transfer at adjacent carbon active sites, reduce the formation barrier of OOH* intermediates, and induce efficient 2e– ORR activity. Concurrently, the polarity and steric effects of functional groups induce structural evolution in COFs from spherical, rod-like to spiderweb-like architectures, wherein the interconnected network of COF-NO2 substantially enhances the diffusion efficiency of reactants and products. This synergy between electronic structure and macroscopic morphology enables COF-NO2 to achieve 94% H2O2 selectivity and a high production rate of 10.5 mol gcat–1 h–1 with sustained stability. This work not only provides outstanding catalysts for efficient electrochemical H2O2 synthesis but also clarifies functional group-induced electronic and morphological modulation, offering a novel paradigm for the rational design of porous catalytic materials.

paper.title: Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry for Characterization of Ir-Based Catalysts for PEM Water Electrolyzers
paper.abstract: Abstract Iridium-based catalysts remain essential for enabling durable oxygen evolution in proton-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs), yet their surface and subsurface chemistries remain insufficiently resolved by conventional characterization methods. Here, we establish time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS), combined with multivariate analysis, as a framework for deconvoluting chemical-, structural-, and depth-dependent features across commercial IrOx powders spanning amorphous and rutile phases. Static and Ar cluster-sputtered ToF-SIMS spectra reveal distinct surface hydroxylation, oxide fragment distributions, and subsurface chemical signatures that differentiate amorphous and rutile IrOx and expose synthesis-dependent residues. Across all powders, surface regions are enriched in hydroxylated IrOx fragments, while subsurface regions show increased reduced Ir species and carbon-based ions. ToF-SIMS fragments are correlated with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) extracted parameters, providing complementary surface chemical information that supports species identification. Finally, integrating ToF-SIMS and XPS descriptors with electrochemical and structural metrics yields a chemically resolved picture linking hydration depth, oxidation state distribution, and structural order to catalytic behavior. This multi-technique, multivariate framework provides insight into the chemical features governing Ir-based OER performance and supports the rational design of robust, efficient catalysts.

paper.title: Interfacial Assembly of 2D Superlattices and Quasicrystals in Binary Nanoparticle Systems with Strong Unlike Interactions
paper.abstract: Two-dimensional nanoparticle (NP) superlattices assembled at fluid–fluid interfaces offer a versatile platform for creating novel materials with applications in plasmonics, spectroscopy, photonics, and catalysis. Recently, we implemented a basin-hopping Monte Carlo approach to identify ground-state configurations of binary NP assemblies at fluid interfaces, which helped predict a range of ordered superlattices, several of which have been observed experimentally. Here, we extend this approach by allowing unlike-particle interactions to vary independently of like-particle interactions, an experimentally relevant feature not considered in our previous work that captures systems such as oppositely charged or chemically dissimilar NPs. We systematically map the resulting phase behavior as a function of particle size ratio, NP-fluid interaction asymmetry, and unlike-interaction strength. The resulting structural transitions reveal how preferred immersion depths, geometric packing, and particle coordination collectively govern assembly. Strengthening unlike-particle attraction shifts phase boundaries toward structures with greater unlike-particle coordination, suppresses phase-separated and like-contact-dominated regions, and stabilizes new crystalline phases inaccessible when unlike interactions are constrained by the like-particle interactions. At strong unlike attraction, additionally varying particle composition gives rise to periodic approximants and quasicrystalline structures with 12-fold and 8-fold symmetry. Collectively, these results establish how particle size asymmetry, differential interfacial affinity, and independently tunable like and unlike interactions can be used to direct structural selection in binary NP assemblies at fluid interfaces.

paper.title: From Physical Principles to ML-Ready Representations: A Unified Framework for Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
paper.abstract: Abstract Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) enables atomic-resolution imaging, but quantitative interpretation remains difficult because tunneling current depends nonlinearly on both surface geometry and electronic structure. We propose a physics-informed representation based on bond valence and tip-height deviation from the covalent surface, which captures the local chemical environment while incorporating permutational invariance and the nearsightedness principle. This representation maps the STM-structure relationship onto a low-dimensional manifold and demonstrates strong transferability across iron carbide stoichiometries and surface orientations. Combined with a compact XGBoost model, it predicts STM images accurately while reducing computation from hours to seconds. Integrated with surface structure filters, the method forms a high-throughput pipeline for candidate screening, image prediction, and experimental validation through an online virtual STM laboratory. The framework can be further expanded in the future to atomic force microscopy and other scanning probe techniques, which establishes a physically grounded framework for efficient, data-driven surface structure determination.

paper.title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
paper.abstract: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.

paper.title: A Simple Model to Predict Complex Coacervation: Forces as Drivers of Phase Change and Structuration
paper.abstract: Abstract Biomolecular condensate formation or coacervation has come to the fore as an extremely attractive research area over the past few years, as these condensates have been conjectured to be the most primitive sort of protocells. One of the most studied coacervation processes is the complex coacervation between polyelectrolytes and oppositely charged small molecules. Among these structures, a very well tested system is the poly-L-Lysine/Adenosine Tri Phosphate (pLL/ATP) coacervate. To understand the condensation process, one needs to unravel the forces which dictate the behaviour of pLL dispersed in water at various temperatures and for various monomer charge fractions which are positively charged. Unlike most simulations which have been performed for biologically relevant proteins, here we have used an included solvent Monte Carlo approach on 10-bead flexible strands as the model pLL molecules, where each bead stands for 3 lysine monomers. Initially we have established the 10-bead model for pLL molecules. We have shown that at high pH, when the positive charges are largely neutralized due to deprotonation of the amine groups in the lysine monomers, the strands show a clear tendency to form bundles of rigid and vertically elongated pLL molecules driven by intermolecular attractions caused by hydrophobic repulsion from the aqueous medium. On switching off the hydrophobic interaction, we see no bundle formation and the screened coulomb repulsions dominate pushing the strands away from each other, underscoring the essential role of hydrophobic interaction in pLL structuration. We see a similar tendency to move away from each other by keeping the charges fixed at high reduced temperatures as well. These results agree nicely with experimental observations of the different phases of pLL, in particular the formation of fibrils at high pH and room temperature. Once we established the pLL model, we introduced negatively charged single ATP beads. Based on the screened coulomb attractions between the polymers and the molecules, we could predict the crossover point where the repulsive regime gets converted into an overall attractive one leading to nucleation and growth, resulting into coacervation. We could, therefore, correlate the ATP/pLL ratio to the forces dictating the phase separation process – for the first time to the best of our knowledge. Additionally, we could find the radial charge and ATP and pLL bead density distributions which allows us to understand the internal structures of the condensates.

paper.title: Rotation‐Coupled Guest Anions Stabilize Polymer Solid‐State Sodium‐Metal Batteries
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Polymer solid‐state sodium‐metal batteries are constrained by sluggish Na + migration and unstable sodium–metal interfaces, both of which are closely associated with poorly regulated solvation chemistry. Here we report a rotation‐coupled guest‐anion strategy in a poly(vinylidene fluoride‐co‐hexafluoropropylene)‐based solid‐state electrolyte (PHSE) using Mg(OTf) 2 . Mg 2+ preferentially coordinates DMF and TFSI − , weakening Na + –TFSI − association and limiting solvent‐derived reactions at the sodium metal anode. OTf − enters the Na + solvation shell as a mobile guest anion. Its C─S rotational axis and equivalent oxygen coordination sites allow conformational rotation to synchronize with Na + hopping along polymer chains. This anchor–rotator chemistry reorganizes Na + coordination, lowers the migration barrier, and promotes an inorganic‐rich, Mg─O‐containing interphase. The optimized electrolyte enables Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 3 ||Na cells to retain 94.2% capacity after 1100 cycles at 2C and supports a 94 mAh pouch cell with stable cycling. It also enables high‐voltage Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 2 O 2 F||Na cells to retain 93.6% capacity after 1000 cycles at 0.5C over 2.5–4.2 V. Comparative evaluation across a total of 20 polymer electrolyte systems with varied polymer matrices and anion structures identifies anion symmetry, rotational periodicity, and finite rotational barriers as molecular criteria for designing stable polymer solid‐state sodium‐metal batteries.

paper.title: Directing group-free site-selective and stereoretentive C-H amination of alkanes with phenyl triazolinedione (PTAD) as a σ-acid
paper.abstract: 4-Phenyl-1,2,4-triazoline-3,5-dione (PTAD) is known as the most reactive commercially available dienophile, as it rapidly reacts with dienes at low temperatures and high dilution. In general terms, PTAD is a very soft Lewis acid, with a strong affinity towards electron rich alkenes. In this work, we report that the potent π-acid PTAD also shows a very useful and general σ-acid reactivity towards electron rich C(sp3)-H bonds, opening up its use in alkane amination reactions, as well as in late stage functionalization applications. The experimental observations over a wide range of alkanes, as well as in more functionalized substrates, indicate a carbocationic mechanism involving a hydride ion transfer of the alkane substrate to PTAD. The carbocation is very transient, as C-N bond formation proceeds generally with retention of the original configuration of a stereogenic carbon. The reaction can be run at high conversion of the alkane substrate using a catalytic amount of a gold(I)-catalyst combined with a mild proton donor such as hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP). The reaction can often fully discriminate between very similar C-H bonds, such as cyclic alkanes over linear ones, equatorial C-H bonds over axial ones and tertiary over secondary ones. These observed reactivity orders closely follow expected trends in carbocation stability, offering a conveniently predictability. This novel C-H functionalization method does not require extensive catalyst or reagent design and offers good complementary to more conventional C-H activation or amination methodologies.

paper.title: Tuning Second-Sphere Amine Basicity to Modulate Hydride Intermediates and Selectivity in Molecular Manganese Bipyridine CO2 Electroreduction
paper.abstract: Abstract Manganese bipyridine tricarbonyl complexes represent a prominent class of molecular electrocatalysts for efficient and selective CO2-to-CO conversion. Recent efforts have sought to redirect product selectivity toward HCOOH by incorporating second-sphere amine proton relays. However, how the physicochemical properties of second-sphere amines govern catalytic activity and selectivity remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we report a new manganese bipyridine complex bearing 2-(pyrrolidin-1-ylmethyl)phenyl substituents at the 6,6′-positions and systematically evaluate its performance against the diethylamine- and morpholine-functionalized analogs to elucidate the role of second-sphere amine basicity on CO2 reduction. The pyrrolidine-functionalized catalyst achieves near-unity selectivity for HCOOH in acetonitrile with a Faradaic efficiency of 92%, outperforming the corresponding diethylamine (71%) and morpholine (23%) derivatives. This complex also displays outstanding catalytic activity with maximum turnover frequencies of 2300 s–1 and up to 70,000 s–1 under low- and high-overpotential conditions, respectively, ranking among the most active manganese bipyridine catalysts for CO2-to-HCOOH conversion. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the pyrrolidine groups function as proton relays, facilitating proton transfer to the manganese center and promoting formation of the key Mn-hydride intermediate for CO2-to-HCOOH conversion. Density functional theory calculations further demonstrate that the stronger basicity of the pyrrolidine functionality lowers the energy barriers for amine protonation and subsequent intramolecular proton transfer by 3–6 kcal mol–1 relative to the less basic diethylamine and morpholine analogs. Overall, this work establishes second-sphere amine basicity as a key molecular parameter for tuning both activity and product selectivity in the development of molecular CO2 reduction catalysts.

paper.title: Symmetric versus asymmetric electron transfer in symmetric molecules
paper.abstract: Photoinduced electron transfer (ET) in symmetric donor-acceptor-donor (D-A-D) or acceptor-donor-acceptor (A-D-A) molecules attracts attention due to applications in advanced materials. It is normally assumed that ET occurs asymmetrically, from one donor to acceptor, thus breaking molecular symmetry and resulting in a dipole moment in the excited state. However, the symmetry can be preserved with symmetric ET from both donors, leading to a nondipolar state with a high quadrupole moment. Here we report on symmetric ET in a D-A-D probe, 5,5'-di(9H-carbazol-9-yl)-2,2'-bipyridine. This probe is weakly solvatochromic in absorption, but highly solvatochromic in emission, revealing a nonlinear spectral shift and strong decay of the oscillator strength in solvents of increasing polarity. We develope a 3-excited-state model that fits the data quite well for symmetric ET, while no reasonable fit is possible for asymmetric ET. The model predicts the symmetric ET to be barrierless and ultrafast, in good agreement with observations.

paper.title: Engineering Intrinsic Mixed Sodium Ionic–Electronic Conductivity in a Nickel Bis(diimine) Metal–Organic Framework
paper.abstract: Abstract Mixed ionic–electronic conductors (MIECs) are highly desirable for a wide range of electronic applications, however, developing single-phase MIECs with intrinsic transport properties under ambient conditions remains challenging. Herein, we report a Na+-ion and electron mixed-conducting metal–organic framework (MOF), Ni-HITP-SO3Na, by tethering anionic sulfonate side chains with Na+ counterions onto the 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexaiminotriphenylene (HITP) ligand of a d-π conjugated nickel bis(diimine)-based framework. Ni-HITP-SO3Na is highly crystalline with honeycomb networks and microporous with surface area of 412 m2 g–1. Remarkably, Ni-HITP-SO3Na exhibits dual transport without relying on conductive fillers, guest electrolytes, or external ion sources. Four-probe measurements reveal a high electronic conductivity of 0.7 ± 0.3 S cm–1, and DC polarization yields a sodium ionic conductivity of (3.7 ± 0.7) × 10–6 S cm–1 at room temperature in the solid state, which can be further improved to (1.5 ± 0.4) × 10–5 S cm–1 with the assistance of solvents. These results, to the best of our knowledge, demonstrate the first MOF that intrinsically combines electronic and sodium ionic conduction, delivering competitive mixed conductivity among reported MIECs, particularly under ambient temperature. The mixed conductivity originates from the intact d–π conjugation for electronic transport and the sulfonate-functionalized pore walls that afford low-barrier Na+ pathways via a relay transport mechanism involving transient bridging coordination between neighboring sulfonate groups. This work highlights embedding ion-transport functionality directly into conductive MOF backbones as an effective route to structurally well-defined, highly porous framework MIECs for electrochemical and iontronic devices.
