paper.title: Enhancing the Computational Efficiency of Aircraft Assembly Simulations Using Deep Learning Warm-Start
paper.abstract: Abstract In modeling the assembly processes of aircraft structures, multiple solutions of quadratic programming problems of a special type are required. Contact problems of stress-strain analysis of structures are reduced to such problems. These numerical models serve as core components of the aircraft assembly digital twin. Despite the use of specialized accelerated solvers, the solution time can be significant, especially for large-scale problems, since the runtime of any solver grows polynomially with increasing problem dimension. One of the acceleration techniques consists of employing initial guesses close to the problem solution, constructed using a neural network. The network is trained on data obtained by solving a large number of problems with synthetic input data. It is known that a finite multilayer perceptron with ReLU activation is capable of accurately reproducing the dependence of the solution of a quadratic programming problem on its input data. In this connection, multi-label classification machine learning models intended for detecting contact in potential contact node pairs are considered. The architecture of the neural network is selected experimentally, and its influence on prediction quality and solver speedup is discussed. The proposed deep learning warm-start method utilizes neural-network-generated initial guesses to accelerate the quadratic programming solver. Evaluated within the context of aerospace informatics, this approach has demonstrated high efficiency on aircraft assembly models. Recommendations are provided for selecting the model architecture and its quantitative characteristics to achieve a balance between the initial guess construction speed and its accuracy.

paper.title: Ultrafast coherent vibrational dynamics and structural rearrangement following photodetachment of the aqueous adenine anion
paper.abstract: Understanding the elementary processes that follow the interaction of ionizing radiation with biomolecules is of fundamental importance in radiation chemistry and radiation biology. Nucleobases are a class of biomolecules that are of particular interest in these fields due to their significance as the building blocks of DNA and the role of nucleobase radicals in DNA damage. Here, femtosecond optical pump–probe spectroscopy is employed to study the ultrafast vibrational wave packet dynamics of the aqueous adenine radical (Ade[-H]•) induced by photodetachment. Strong-field photodetachment of the aqueous adenine anion (Ade[-H]−) by intense, few-cycle pump pulses drives the formation of the hydrated electron and aqueous Ade[-H]•. Absorption signatures of the hydrated electron and Ade[-H]• are observed in the transient absorption spectra, probed in the visible–near-infrared and ultraviolet range. The pronounced modulations present in the transient absorption spectra encode vibrational wave packet dynamics of aqueous Ade[-H]•. This vibrational wave packet motion is resolved into ten vibrational modes along which structural reorganization occurs upon photodetachment. Density functional theory calculations assign the observed vibrational modes and quantify the extent of structural rearrangement following photodetachment. This work provides insights into the ultrafast structural dynamics that accompany the ionization of biomolecules in an aqueous environment.

paper.title: De Novo Engineering High‐Density Proximal Copper Single Atoms for Enhanced C─C Coupling in CO 2 Electroreduction
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Copper‐based single‐atom catalysts (SACs) are promising for the electrochemical CO 2 reduction reaction, yet their multicarbon production remains restricted by the inherent trade‐off among atomic loading, dispersion, and proximity required for efficient C─C coupling. In this study, we develop a de novo coordination‐site and geometry engineering strategy to construct high‐density proximal Cu SACs for improving CO 2 ‐to‐C 2+ electroreduction. Flexible molecular building blocks rich in N/O coordination motifs assemble into wrinkled 2D networks and further hierarchically organize into a 3D nanoflower framework, where isolated Cu sites with high loading of 14 wt% are anchored via robust N/O coordination. The structural bending brings adjacent Cu atoms into close proximity (∼2.6 Å). Competitive N/O coordination generates asymmetric and low‐coordinated microenvironments, promoting *CO intermediate stabilization and subsequent C─C coupling. The optimized catalyst achieves a C 2+ Faradaic efficiency of 81.34% at 500 mA·cm −2 , including 51% ethylene selectivity, with stable operation exceeding 100 h. This work sheds light on structural dimensional control and microenvironment engineering for promoting cooperative catalysis in single‐atom systems, offering new opportunities for efficient multicarbon electrosynthesis.

paper.title: Galvanic Coupling Links Heterogeneous and Molecular Palladium Catalysis in Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
paper.abstract: Thermochemical catalytic reactions are often composed of coupled electrochemical redox reactions, which may even generate the active catalyst itself. Here we show that oxygen reduction on heterogeneous palladium drives corrosion of Pd(0) through galvanic coupling: electrons released by Pd(0) oxidation are consumed by oxygen reduction on the same catalyst, and the soluble Pd(II) forms a homogeneous complex which catalyzes benzyl alcohol oxidation. Combining corrosion measurements with quantification of Pd(II) and reaction products, we find that supplying more oxygen raises the catalyst potential and accelerates Pd(II) generation and alcohol oxidation. Applying equivalent electrochemical potentials in the absence of oxygen reproduces Pd(II) generation and alcohol oxidation with similar sensitivity to the catalyst potential. Diverting the anodic reaction to a sacrificial anode suppresses Pd(II) supply and thus the thermochemical reaction rate. Hence, the primary role of oxygen is to set the potential for generating the active catalyst, while palladium corrosion is the kinetic link to thermochemical turnover. Together, our results show that galvanic coupling provides a framework that links electrochemistry and thermochemical catalysis.

paper.title: Sulfur Clusters Anchored on Carbon Enables High‐Loading, Low‐Coordination Noble Metal Cluster Catalysts for Electrocatalysis
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT A rational catalyst design demands a versatile platform integrating high intrinsic activity, optimal atomic utilization, high loading, and stability. We report an ultra‐stable three‐dimensional sulfur cluster anchored on a carbon scaffold, which forms a multi‐directional anchoring network for noble metals, effectively overcoming the inherent short‐range limitation of strong metal‐support interactions. A 40 wt% Platinum cluster catalyst with cluster size of over 1.5 nm and an average Pt–Pt coordination number of ∼3 was successfully fabricated. The resulting Pt/SCC achieved an overpotential of only 3.9 mV at 10 mA/cm 2 with a mass activity (MA) of 17.5 A/mg Pt in 0.5 M H 2 SO 4 , and requires just 9.9 mV at 10 mA/cm 2 and a MA of 0.47 A/mg Pt in 1.0 M KOH. It also shows super durability with marginal loss in activity after 100 000 cyclic voltammetry cycles in both conditions. Pt/SCC delivers exceptional atomic utilization, slashing electrolyzer Pt loading by >50% without compromising long‐term durability.

paper.title: Probabilistic algorithms for Ising machines from optimization to generative AI
paper.abstract: Ising machines could accelerate hard optimization and sampling tasks, but their impact depends on algorithm–hardware co-design. This Review surveys portable probabilistic methods, from annealing and tempering to Probabilistic Approximate Optimization Algorithm and generative AI hybrids, arguing that principled algorithms and specialized hardware should evolve together to expand capability, scalability and practical adoption.

paper.title: Edge-Aware Graph Attention Networks for Interpreting Biophysical Mechanisms from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
paper.abstract: Graph attention networks (GATs) are emerging as powerful aritficial intelligence (AI) tools for learning biomolecular dynamics, yet extracting mechanistic insight from learned attention remains challenging. Here, we present an interpretable AI approach that combines molecular dynamics prediction with mechanistic interpretation through attention-derived communication networks. We develop three edge-aware GAT models - Edge-Conditioned, Edge-Injected, and Edge-Gated - that differ in how edge information is incorporated during message passing. Relative to a standard GAT, our edge-aware models improve coordinate prediction while recovering complementary aspects of residue communication. Application to Chignolin and HIV-1 protease demonstrates their ability to characterize communication networks underlying protein folding, allostery, and mutation-induced functional remodeling. Analysis of the communication networks using graph-based descriptors of communication throughput, intensity, and relay revealed that the Edge-Conditioned model preferentially emphasizes communication hubs characterized by high communication throughput and intensity, the Edge-Injected model preferentially highlights high-intensity communication within functionally important regions, and the Edge-Gated model most clearly resolves long-range communication relay. Overall, this approach provides an interpretable AI strategy for uncovering the communication mechanisms that underlie folding, allostery, and long-range signal propagation in molecular machines, while also supporting AI-guided modulation of biomolecular function and rational protein engineering.

paper.title: Termination controlled Phase-Pure Ti3C2Tx MXenes Towards Efficient Electrocatalysis
paper.abstract: Abstract MXenes are promising electrocatalysts for sustainable hydrogen generation, but establishing reliable structure–activity relationships to achieve phase purity and control surface terminations remains challenging. Here, we report phase-pure Ti3C2-F and Ti3C2-O MXenes synthesised via a molten-salt process, achieving purities >99.6%. Ti₃C₂-F exhibits excellent performance in the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic solutions, with a very low overpotential of 86 mV at 10 mA cm-2 and a Tafel slope of 55 mV dec-1. Ti₃C₂-O shows bifunctional catalytic activity in alkaline conditions, with HER and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) overpotentials of 76 and 134 mV at 10 mA cm⁻², and Tafel slopes of 86 and 102 mV dec⁻¹, respectively. Their outstanding activities and stabilities are attributed to phase-purity and tunable surface terminations, enabling different pathways for hydrogen and hydroxide activation. These findings not only elucidate the underlying reaction mechanisms but also demonstrate the potential of termination-controlled MXenes for efficient energy conversion.

paper.title: Adaptive TinyML at the Edge: A Multi-Seed Empirical Study of Drift, Robustness, Energy, Federated Learning, and Explainability
paper.abstract: Abstract A multi-seed (N=5) empirical study of five adaptive TinyML challenges on synthetic sensor data. Latency and memory are analytically simulated. Key results with paired t-tests (df=4): (1) Drift: TinyOL achieved 0.851+/-0.052 post-drift accuracy vs 0.563+/-0.033 for static (mean diff=0.288, 95%CI=[0.199, 0.376], p=0.0008). (2) Quantisation: for this input-feature quantisation scheme on synthetic data, 8-bit accuracy (0.979+/-0.008 clean) was not significantly different from the unquantised reference (p=0.099). 4-bit clean accuracy was significantly lower (p=0.0273). These results apply to input-feature quantisation only and do not generalise to weight quantisation or integer-only MCU inference. (3) Energy (simulated): adaptive switching at T=20% saves 29% vs fixed-large (130 vs 184 mJ); T=40% and T=60% save 42% (106 mJ). Both adaptive policies exceed fixed-small accuracy. (4) Federated: FL-only and FL+TL show indistinguishable cross-client std (0.081+/-0.006 each). The earlier FL+TL equity claim is retracted. (5) Explainability: neural baseline accuracy significantly exceeded fuzzy tuner (mean diff=0.027, 95%CI=[0.003, 0.051], p=0.0351) while the fuzzy model scored 2.4x higher on a structural interpretability proxy (not user-validated).

paper.title: From Promotion to Poisoning: Temperature- and Coverage-Dependent Effects of Trace Fe on the Hydrogen Evolution Activity of Pt
paper.abstract: Trace iron impurities can strongly alter the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet how temperature governs their surface accumulation and kinetic consequences remains poorly understood. Here, the influence of 0–60 ppb Fe impurities on polycrystalline Pt was systematically examined in 0.1 M KOH over 280–336 K. Fe addition progressively suppressed the hydrogen underpotential-deposition (Hupd) charge, indicating blockage of Pt sites by Fe-derived surface species, while this suppression was substantially mitigated at elevated temperature. Despite this site blocking, 10–20 ppb Fe enhanced the HER current, whereas further Fe addition caused pronounced deactivation, particularly at 280–298 K. Wide-potential-range voltammetry revealed electrochemical responses consistent with hydroxide-like Fe species undergoing an Fe(II)/Fe(III)-type redox transition, with the Fe-associated anodic charge decreasing markedly at 336 K. Apparent thermodynamic analyses further indicated that Fe-induced site blocking cannot be described by adsorption on a single population of independent, equivalent sites. Most importantly, correlation of the Hupd-derived blocked-site fraction with the Tafel slope revealed three coverage-dependent regimes: kinetic promotion at low Fe coverage, predominantly site-number-limited deactivation at intermediate coverage, and severe kinetic inhibition at high coverage. These results demonstrate that trace Fe does not behave as a simple inert poison but dynamically modifies the Pt/Fe-derived interface in a coverage- and temperature-dependent manner. The findings establish electrolyte temperature and trace-impurity coverage as coupled parameters controlling alkaline HER kinetics on Pt.

paper.title: Microstructure–Driven Degradation Mechanisms in High-Nickel NMC Cathodes for Lithium-Ion Batteries
paper.abstract: Mechanical degradation in high-nickel layered oxide cathodes is closely associated with anisotropic lattice-parameter changes during electrochemical cycling, yet how cathode microstructure size influences the resulting crystallographic deformation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate two LiNi0.90Mn0.05Co0.05O2 (NMC955) cathodes with comparable secondary-particle sizes but different average grain sizes (1.0 and 0.5 µm). The fine-grained cathode delivers 30% higher initial discharge capacity, 40% lower voltage polarization, improved rate capability, and 13% higher capacity retention after 100 cycles. Despite its superior electrochemical performance, the fine-grained material exhibits approximately 1.23 times higher mean kernel average misorientation after 100 cycles, together with higher estimated geometrically necessary dislocation density, indicating greater average local lattice curvature. The coarse-grained cathode shows pronounced localization of crystallographic misorientation near grain boundaries and secondary-particle peripheries, whereas the fine-grained cathode exhibits a more spatially distributed misorientation response. Complementary chemo-mechanical simulations reproduce the grain-size-dependent trends in lattice curvature and reveal differences in the spatial distribution of plastic strain associated with the different grain sizes. After 100 cycles, the coarse-grained cathode undergoes extensive intergranular cracking and secondary-particle fragmentation, while the fine-grained cathode largely preserves its structural integrity. These findings identify the spatial localization of cycling-induced crystallographic misorientation, rather than its average magnitude alone, as a pivotal variable for electrode design.

paper.title: Immunodetection of a Cell-Surface Biomarker via the Freezing of Supercooled Water Droplets
paper.abstract: Immunolabels traditionally detect biomarkers via a color change or fluorescence. The frequently weak signals from low biomarker concentrations prompted the development of numerous enzymatic amplification strategies. Although very effective for signal generation, these strategies increase the complexity, cost, and time required for immunoassays. What if water itself could generate and self-amplify a signal to detect a biomarker? Here, we demonstrate that it is possible to detect a cell-surface protein biomarker by inducing the phase change from water to ice in supercooled water droplets. Relative to enzymatic amplification, this phase change has the potential for orders-of-magnitude larger amplification factors on orders-of-magnitude shorter time scales. We engineered a recombinant ice-nucleating protein (rINpro), based on the bacterial protein InaZ, that binds to an antigen via a tetrameric antibody complex. Breast cancer cells expressing the Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (HER2) antigen were adopted as a model system. Arrays with 96 × 10 μL droplets containing cells immunolabeled with rINpro froze at a higher average median freezing temperature (–11.2 ± 0.5 °C) than droplets with unlabeled cells (–23.4 ± 1.3 °C) and non-target cells (–25.1 ± 0.6 °C). High-speed videos of freezing droplets confirmed that the labeled cells triggered the freezing and nucleated macroscopic ice formation. As few as ca. 500 target cells were successfully detected among 10,000 non-target cells, and selective naked-eye detection of target cells was possible with a household freezer and fixed cooling period. The “cryo-assay” in this study represents a completely new approach to sensitive biomarker detection. With further development, it has vast potential for the detection of low-abundance biomarkers in research, clinical, and point-of-care immunoassay applications.

paper.title: Probing the Softer-acid Nature of 102No2+ Compared to Alkaline Earth Metal ions via Synergistic Extraction with Sulfur Donor on Crown Ether Supported Resin
paper.abstract: Unlike other f block elements that typically exhibit +3 or higher oxidation states, nobelium (No, atomic number = 102) exists predominantly as the divalent cation in aqueous solutions. While No2+ has long been considered chemically analogous to Ca2+ and Sr2+, strong relativistic effects are predicted to alter its reactivity. In our previous study, the soft metal ion behavior of No2+ was demonstrated through complexation with crown ethers. Prompted by this implication, in this study, we performed online solid-liquid extraction experiments of 255No by employing diethyl dithiophosphate (DEDTP−) as a soft sulfur-donor ligand to probe the softer Lewis acid character of No relative to alkaline earth metals via No–S bonding. Here we report the results of the experiments and relativistic DFT calculations. In the Sr resin/HDEDTP (aqueous) system, No2+ behaves in a manner distinct from Ca2+ and Sr2+, resembling Ba2+ and Ra2+. No2+ exhibits a significantly higher extraction efficiency in the HDEDTP system than Sr2+, confirming enhanced soft Lewis acid character. The computed Gibbs free energies of extraction-complex formation are consistent with the experimental ΔG trend, validating the theoretical model. The optimized geometry revealed a No–S bond shorter than ionic radius trends, indicating stronger bonding. We attribute this distinctive behavior to unique electronic states of No. Specifically, higher electron gain in the d-orbital, stronger relativistic 7s stabilization, and closer 5f energy matching synergistically enhance covalent character of No–S bonding.

paper.title: Internally Polarized Covalent Organic Frameworks: A Design Strategy for Single-Component Photovoltaics
paper.abstract: Molecular dipoles generate strong electric fields on the sub-nanometer scale, the very scale on which photogenerated excitons in organic semiconductors are bound. Harnessing such fields to drive charge generation throughout a photovoltaic material, however, has not been achieved. Realizing this would require ordering vast numbers of molecules throughout the bulk, which is precisely the structural control offered by covalent organic frameworks (COFs). In this work, we explore in silico the design of COFs that exploit internal-field-driven exciton dissociation, and show how they can be used to overcome a central challenge in single-component organic photovoltaics: converting strongly bound Frenkel excitons into long-lived separated charges. Using models that span from a single donor–bridge–acceptor unit to the full periodic material, we follow the photoexcitation process through its full cycle, from light absorption, through exciton dissociation, to charge recombination, and in turn isolate the effect of internal polarization at each stage. We show that polarization is essential for efficient exciton dissociation, preventing the kinetic hole trapping prevalent in an unpolarized analog. To investigate the recombination process on the nanosecond timescale, we develop a dedicated nonadiabatic molecular dynamics protocol, which, validated against an experimentally known donor–acceptor COF built from the same units, reproduces its charge-carrier lifetime with high accuracy. Applying it to the newly designed systems, we predict an almost 40-fold increase in charge-carrier lifetime. Our results identify internal polarization as a promising, unexplored approach to organic photovoltaic design and demonstrate how electronic-structure engineering at the building-block level translates into material-level performance.

paper.title: Investigation of NaxFePO4 systems prepared by a modified Pechini sol-gel method as possible cathode materials for high voltage Na-ion batteries
paper.abstract: An uncomplicated modification of a Pechini assisted sol-gel process in water-polyol solutions is proposed for the synthesis of Na-Fe phosphate powders with different Na-ion content as cathode materials for sodium ion batteries (SIBs). Depending on the pH-values, X-ray diffraction detected the formation of Na-poor olivine-like o-NaFePO4 orthorhombic phase and o-FePO4 nanocrystalline structure. The cyclic voltammetry of the SIBs shows reduction peaks at ~2.23 V (x = 1.0) and ~2.12 V (x = 1.2) vs. Na/Na+ for pH < 3, and between 2.8 V - ~3.0 V (x = 1.0) for pH = 5 respectively. For x = 1.2, several redox peaks observed for pH=5 are assigned to a single-phase reaction (at ~2.5 V vs. Na/Na+) and two-phase reactions (at 3.0–3.25 V). Redox peaks above 4.5 V are more likely associated with Fe3+/Fe4+ redox coupling. A good cyclability is observed for the cathodes synthesized at both the pH values even by charging the batteries to the upper cut-off 4.8 V. The Na-cathode materials prepared under milder conditions showed the highest specific capacity of 40 mAhg-1.

paper.title: Time-Dependent Wave-Packet Approach to Reactions for Quantum Computation
paper.abstract: We describe a method for obtaining the scattering matrix for nuclear or chemical reactions on a finite lattice. Aside from the preparation of the initial and final states as wave packets, the only other operation required is unitary time evolution, making this approach ideal for simulations on quantum hardware. The central quantity is a time-dependent overlap between incoming and outgoing wave packets whose Fourier transform corresponds to the scattering matrix at fixed energy, from which one can calculate elastic and inelastic cross sections for reactions involving two interacting clusters. Working in Cartesian coordinates enables an efficient encoding of the problem on quantum hardware via the first quantization mapping, with favorable qubit scaling for describing asymptotic scattering states. Within this framework, we describe a quantum algorithm for probing the scattering amplitude through different angles, including the forward direction, which provides access to the total cross section via the optical theorem. We demonstrate our methods through a series of numerical examples, for both elastic and inelastic processes, comparing against exact calculations. The techniques we describe can more readily be extended to a large number of constituent particles than other existing approaches, once fault-tolerant quantum hardware becomes available.

paper.title: QPE-Inspired Adaptive Phase Tracking for Discrete-Variable Quantum Key Distribution under Unitary Channel Drift
paper.abstract: Abstract Environmental phase drift is a critical impairment in discrete-variable quantum key distribution (DV-QKD), particularly when phase coherence is required for superposition-basis measurements or entanglement-based correlations. This work proposes a QPE-inspired adaptive phase tracking framework for mitigating unitary channel drift in BB84 and BBM92 protocols. Across both evaluated phase-drift regimes, the proposed QPE-inspired tracking framework reduced the mean QBER by factors ranging from approximately 5× to 10× relative to the corresponding untracked baselines. The proposed approach combines a discretized quantum phase-sensing stage with a classical feedback loop, enabling adaptive estimation and compensation of residual phase rotations at the receiver. Unlike full quantum state tomography, the method is designed to operate as a lightweight hybrid quantum-classical feedback mechanism, using phase-sensitive calibration information without explicitly reconstructing the transmitted quantum states. State-vector simulations implemented in Qiskit Aer compare untracked BB84 and BBM92 baselines with the proposed QPE-inspired tracking architecture under stochastic phase drift. Simulations with \(\:N=1000\) transmission rounds show that the proposed framework maintains the QBER below the 11% asymptotic threshold for both BB84 and BBM92 under two phase-drift regimes: a moderate fiber-like regime with \(\:\gamma\:=0.04\) rad/round and \(\:{\sigma\:}_{ch}\in\:\left[\text{0,0.35}\right]\) rad, and a high-drift aeronautical regime with \(\:\gamma\:=0.15\) rad/round and \(\:{\sigma\:}_{ch}\in\:\left[\text{0.02,0.25}\right]\) rad. In contrast, the corresponding untracked baselines remain above the threshold and yield vanishing asymptotic secret-key rates. A further intercept-resend scenario is evaluated to verify that non-unitary adversarial disturbances remain observable in the total QBER. The proposed framework is therefore positioned as a simulation-based phase-tracking strategy for DV-QKD under unitary channel noise, rather than as a complete security proof against general attacks.

paper.title: Fe-dopant site occupancy in Co3O4: evidence of isovalent substitution and short-range association at octahedral sites
paper.abstract: Understanding how dopant site occupancy influences the behavior of spinel oxides is essential for tailoring their functional properties. Here, we combine DFT+U calculations with computational and experimental Co K-edge XANES spectroscopy to investigate the structural, electronic, and magnetic effects of Fe incorporation into Co3O4. The results indicate a strong energetic preference for isovalent substitution, with Fe3+ preferentially occupying octahedral Co3+ sites. This preference becomes more pronounced with increasing dopant concentration, leading to a clear stability hierarchy in which short-distance double-octahedral configurations are energetically favored. Dopant–dopant interactions further influence this stability landscape, promoting attractive coupling for octahedral and mixed-site configurations, while tetrahedral Fe3+ exhibits weak or slightly repulsive interactions. These trends are reflected in the magnetic properties, with octahedral Fe inducing stronger local magnetic moments compared to tetrahedral substitution. The calculated XANES spectra reveal site-dependent modifications of the Co pre-edge features that can be related to changes in the local electronic structure induced by Fe doping. However, these spectral changes should be interpreted qualitatively in light of known limitations of the theoretical approach. Overall, this study highlights the central role of dopant site occupancy, in addition to dopant concentration, in tuning the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of Co3O4 spinels.

paper.title: First Experimental Evidence of Helicon Current Drive
paper.abstract: Helicon current drive is an attractive solution for driving current to sustain steady state tokamak operation in reactor conditions. Dedicated DIII-D experiments have been conducted with a MW-level helicon system and successfully demonstrated core power deposition and current drive with helicon waves launched via a traveling wave antenna. The profile of the measured electron temperature response to helicon power injection is in good agreement with time-dependent integrated modeling that incorporates ray tracing and the effects of thermal transport simultaneously. When the helicon power is injected continuously to drive co-$I_p$ current, the reconstructed safety factor profile flattens significantly faster and sawteeth are triggered earlier than in comparison shots where the helicon is replaced by a comparable amount of electron cyclotron heating. Calculation of the helicon-driven current profile yields a peaked profile in the core, consistent with the observed power deposition profile and in good agreement with ray tracing predictions. Taken together, these experimental results represent strong evidence for the first definitive observation of auxiliary current drive due to helicon waves on any device.

paper.title: Scrambling-free synthesis of heteroleptic silylium ions by halide abstraction from halosilanes
paper.abstract: Abstract Heteroleptic silylium ions with different substituents at the silicon atom are generally not accessible using established tools for producing such reactive intermediates because substituent exchange reactions occur in acidic media, leading to homoleptic silylium ions with three identical alkyl and aryl substituents, respectively. Here we report a broadly applicable route to heteroleptic silylium ions using halosilanes as silylium ion precursors, which are less prone to that scrambling process. While this deceptively simple method has failed so far owing to the lack of a suitable halide-abstracting agent, superhalophilic halogen-substituted silylium ions enable smooth halide abstraction from a diverse set of halosilanes at ambient temperature without substituent redistribution. Accordingly, this approach provides access to essentially any heteroleptic acyclic as well as cyclic silylium-ion motif from common halosilanes, including trialkyl-, dialkyl(aryl)-, alkyldiaryl- and triaryl-substituted congeners. Computational calculations reveal the mechanism of heteroleptic silylium-ion formation and the origin of the suppressed substituent-scrambling process.

paper.title: Global optimization workflow with compact graph neural networks for comprehensive transition-state mapping
paper.abstract: Abstract Locating the transition states in them remains a central computational bottleneck, particularly in heterogeneous catalysis where reference data are scarce and the configurations that matter are not known in advance. Most machine-learning approaches to transition-state prediction pursue increasingly expressive architectures trained on abundant gas-phase data, a strategy poorly matched to data-limited surface chemistry. We present an integrated workflow that couples our global optimization code with a deliberately compact graph neural network with essential physical invariances encoded into the input representation rather than learned by the network architecture. The global search maps not only ground states but also the low-lying metastable configurations that conventional searches discard. A lightweight network, using 2–3 orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than competing models, predicts transition states for matching configuration pairs. Our results indicate that, in data-scarce scientific domains, matching model capacity to the available data offers a robust and transferable alternative to ever-larger models.

paper.title: Ligand Protonation Tunes Hydride-Transfer Thermochemistry in an Iron Metal-Ligand Cooperative Catalyst
paper.abstract: Cyclopentadienone iron complexes are established metal-ligand cooperative hydrogenation catalysts, yet their bifunctional reactivity complicates the independent evaluation of proton- and hydride-transfer thermodynamics. Here, room-temperature H 2 -splitting enables deconvolution of these contributions, affording a new anionic hydride with a hydricity of 39.0 kcal·mol -1 . Ligand protonation weakens hydride-donor strength by 10 kcal mol -1 , highlighting protonation-state control of reactivity in MLC catalysis.

paper.title: Elucidating Lithium-Ion Dynamics in Highly Concentrated Electrolytes with Markov State Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Highly concentrated electrolytes (HCEs) have attracted considerable attention for lithium batteries owing to their wide electrochemical stability windows and favorable interfacial properties, which originate from their anion-rich solvation structures. The dynamics of lithium ions play a key role for HCEs performance; however, a clear mechanistic understanding of lithium-ion (Li+) transport within percolating ionic networks of HCEs remains elusive. Here, we performed a molecular dynamics simulation on a lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide/1,2-dimethoxyethane (LiFSI/DME) HCE system and then constructed a Markov state model (MSM) using a graph convolutional neural network architecture named GDyNet to investigate the dynamics of lithium ions. The MSM classifies lithium ions into three distinct metastable states based on their local coordination environments: nonsolvated state (State 0), moderately solvated state (State 1), and highly solvated state (State 2), which are kinetically well separated and exhibit distinct dynamic behaviors. Li+ transport in LiFSI/DME HCE is dominated by the self-transitions within each state rather than interstate transitions. During the slow interconversion among the three metastable states, FSI– anions in the coordination shells undergo frequent exchange. The moderately solvated state exhibits the fastest diffusion, followed by the highly solvated state, and the nonsolvated state exhibits the slowest. By integrating the Green–Kubo relation and MSMs, we quantified the relative contributions of these state transitions to Li+ conduction. The transitions from the nonsolvated state contribute negligibly to Li+ conduction, and the dominant contributions originate from the moderately and highly solvated states. The insights obtained from the MSM provide an in-depth mechanistic understanding of Li+ dynamics in HCEs.

paper.title: A Negative Temperature Effect on the Reversible Conversion between Redox Tautomers of CoIII(OH) and CoIV(O) Complexes Bearing a Redox-Non-Innocent Tetraamido Macrocyclic Ligand
paper.abstract: Abstract Elucidating highly reactive intermediates in catalytic reactions relies heavily on cryogenic trapping techniques, where intermediates observed in solution are generally assumed to remain unchanged upon flash-freezing at 77 K. Herein, we demonstrate a striking exception to this long-standing assumption. A cobalt(III)-hydroxo complex bearing a tetraamido macrocyclic ligand radical cation (1: [(TAML•+)CoIII(OH)]−), which is readily observed in solution, is rapidly and quantitatively converted upon freezing to the corresponding cobalt(IV)-oxo complex containing a protonated TAML ligand (2: [(H-TAML)CoIV(O)(HOTf)]−) in the presence of HOTf in acetone. Remarkably, the conversion of 1 to 2 exhibits a negative temperature effect, becoming significantly faster at lower temperatures. Eyring analysis afforded activation parameters of ΔH‡ = −6.0(5) kcal mol–1 and ΔS‡ = −96(7) cal K–1 mol–1. Mechanistic studies reveal that this interconversion proceeds through an acid-assisted proton-coupled electron-transfer (PCET) pathway in which HOTf binding to the redox noninnocent TAML•+ ligand promotes intramolecular electron transfer from the CoIII center to the TAML•+ ligand, coupled with proton transfer from the hydroxo ligand to the TAML framework to produce 2. While the equilibrium constant for the exothermic binding of HOTf increases at lower temperatures, the intrinsic rate constant of the subsequent intramolecular PCET step decreases. Consequently, the overall conversion becomes faster upon cooling because of the interplay between these two processes. This study provides the first example of a negative temperature effect on the reversible conversion between two redox tautomers, demonstrating that cryogenic cooling can drive, rather than simply trap, the interconversion of transient intermediates.

The built-in chemical asymmetry enables directional ion transport, enhanced osmotic energy conversion and robust operation under strongly acidic conditions.

paper.title: Selective Cancer Cell Killing via a Fluorofoldamer‐Based Proton Channel That Triggers Ferroptosis
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT We report a new class of aromatic foldamer‐based artificial proton channels incorporating fluorinated building blocks, which exhibit high proton transport efficiency and selectivity. The lead channel, 2 , shows outstanding proton transport activity (EC 50 = 13.1–14.7 nM) and high selectivity (H + /Cl − = 249.7; H + /Na + = 23.9; H + /K + = 45.0), forming transmembrane channels without compromising membrane integrity or facilitating the transport of competing ions. By exploiting the unique acidic tumor microenvironment, 2 mediates proton influx to acidify the intracellular environment of cancer cells, inducing cell death via ferroptosis. This is evidenced by the downregulation of AKR1B1 and GPX4, corresponding increases in reactive oxygen species (ROS) and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, and lipid remodeling. Accordingly, 2 exhibits potent cytotoxicity across multiple cancer cell lines (IC 50 < 10 µM) and significantly suppresses tumor growth in vivo without observable systemic toxicity. This work establishes the first artificial proton channel (APC) that induces ferroptosis via channel‐mediated intracellular acidification, offering a membrane‐targeted anticancer strategy with low propensity for drug resistance.

paper.title: Whole-Enzyme Reactive Free-Energy Simulations with a Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potential: Catalytic Mechanism and Mutational Effects of PETase
paper.abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) have emerged as powerful tools for atomistic simulations that achieve quantum mechanical accuracy at significantly reduced computational cost. Yet, their direct application to complex enzymatic reactions remains challenging owing to the immense size of solvated enzyme systems and the scarcity of transition-state structures in training data. In this study, we demonstrate that PFP (PreFerred Potential), a pretrained uMLIP across 96 elements in nature, simulates the complete hydrolytic cycle of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) catalyzed by PETase as a single reactive domain of approximately 20,000 atoms, without multiscale partitioning or system-specific fine-tuning. Umbrella-sampling simulations revealed stepwise mechanisms for both acylation and deacylation through distinct tetrahedral intermediates. The computed rate-limiting deacylation barrier of 20.5 ± 0.3 kcal/mol is in agreement with the range of 18.0–18.7 kcal/mol inferred from experimental turnover numbers. The PFP-based simulations further capture catalytic consequences of point mutations from loss of function (D177N, M132A) to predicted activity enhancement (D157N) and reveal that simultaneous neutralization of three distal acidic residues which are located more than 10 Å from the active site raises the activation barrier due to a collective long-range electrostatic effect that emerges naturally in the partition-free treatment. These findings demonstrate that the pretrained uMLIP, PFP, can provide physically plausible free-energy profiles for enzymatic reaction mechanisms and capture mutational effects, providing a powerful platform for rational enzyme design.

paper.title: Nanoconfinement-cooperated catalysis enables rapid tandem redox kinetics for wide-temperature lithium-sulfur batteries
paper.abstract: The slow kinetics of sulfur cathodes caused by the high energy barriers of Li + desolvation stem primarily from the structure of the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP). Herein, a synergistic strategy combining electrochemical tandem catalysis with spatial nanoconfinement is proposed to regulate the Li(solvent) x + dynamics. As a proof-of-concept, the porous covalent organic framework (denoted as TPBD) decorated MXene is in situ constructed, acting as a tandem kinetic promoter. The theoretical simulations and in situ Raman reveal that the porous TPBD layer confines the bulky Li(solvent) x + species and sieves the spatial structure with accelerated Li + diffusion kinetics. Meanwhile, MXene serves as a negatively charged substrate that helps disrupt anion-solvent interactions and reconstruct the solvation structure at the IHP, thereby enhancing Li + kinetics and sulfur redox reversibility. Encouragingly, the assembled cells demonstrate a superior Li + transference number (0.77), long-term cycling lifespan up to 1000 cycles, as well as excellent areal capacity (>6 mAh cm −2 ) at 0°C and superior rate capability at 50°C under a high sulfur loading of 7.51 mg cm −2 . The as-prepared pouch cell remains stable for over 100 cycles, validating this novel integration of catalysis and nanoconfinement for tandem kinetics in Li-S batteries.

paper.title: High-Density Iridium Single Atoms on Vanadium-Doped TiO2 for Electrochemical Water Oxidation Catalysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Water oxidation in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) uses IrO2 nanoparticles supported on corrosion-resistant TiO2. However, the low conductivity of TiO2 imposes electronic transport limitations that necessitate high Ir loadings for effective catalysis. Here, we present a catalyst design strategy that couples a heavily V-doped TiO2 support with high-density Ir single atoms, enabling water oxidation at minimal Ir loading. In this design, Ti-site-substituted V provides n-type doping, and selective V leaching creates cation vacancies that anchor Ir as isolated atoms. TEM with convolutional neural network (CNN)-based analysis shows Ir single-atom density increases with V content, accompanied by lower charge-transfer resistance and higher Ir-specific activity. The density functional theory indicates that cation-site Ir introduces a midgap state below V 3d levels and shifts neighboring V 3d orbitals toward the Fermi level. Ir1/V-TiO2 achieves 1480 A gIr–1 at 1.55 V vs RHE (1.3 wt % Ir) and demonstrates device-level PEMWE operation at an Ir loading as low as 0.027 mgIr cm–2.

paper.title: Are Molecular Foundation Models Ready for Free Energy Simulations?
paper.abstract: Foundation models for atomistic simulations offer broadly applicable potentialenergy surfaces that can either be applied in a zero-shot manner (without domainspecific retraining) or fine-tuned to the task at hand. Their accuracy is typically judged by energy and force errors on near-equilibrium data, yet it remains largely unclear whether these metrics translate into reliable free-energy landscapes. Here, enhanced sampling can be a particularly demanding test: simulations are driven far from equilibrium into sparsely trained regions and held there over long trajectories, so that small systematic errors in forces or relative energies can accumulate and distort predicted populations, transition pathways, and barriers. We assess several molecular foundation models trained on different dataset sizes and architectures (including models with explicit long-range electrostatics) in prototypical metadynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Our results show that recent foundation models can reproduce simple gas-phase free-energy profiles with near-reference accuracy, while more complex multidimensional and solvated free-energy landscapes remain challenging. However, assessing their performance in these systems is further complicated by limitations in current sampling protocols and the lack of well-defined reference data. These findings highlight the need for more rigorous sampling protocols and reliable benchmarks to systematically assess the accuracy of future molecular foundation models in free-energy calculations.

paper.title: Bioinspired Adaptive Ångström‐Channels in a Hydrogen‐Bonded Metal–Organic Framework for Selective Water Removal From Gas Streams by Molecular Sieving Dehydration
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The removal of water from light hydrocarbons is a critical yet energy‐intensive step in petrochemical processes. Conventional adsorbents often suffer from high regeneration temperatures and undesirable co‐adsorption. Inspired by the selective water transport mechanism of aquaporins, we report a hydrogen‐bonded metal–organic framework, ZNU‐33, featuring bioinspired adaptive one‐dimensional channels. The pore walls are decorated with both positively charged (Hbpa + ) and negatively charged (HEDP 4− ) recognition sites. Using in situ single‐crystal x‐ray diffraction, we captured five phases of ZNU‐33, activated (ZNU‐33‐α), intermediate (ZNU‐33‐β), partially dehydrated (ZNU‐33‐γ and ZNU‐33‐γ2), and fully hydrated ZNU‐33, directly visualizing a water‑triggered structural transition. Structural snapshots reveal water uptake proceeding from free‐channel water to Cu 2+ coordination and then to extended hydrogen‐bonded water chains. ZNU‐33 exhibits high water uptake (9.50 mmol/g at 2.85 kPa and 298 K) and negligible adsorption of CO 2 and all light hydrocarbons. Breakthrough experiments demonstrate efficient water removal under wide flow rates, temperatures, and humidity levels, with water‐adsorption capacity recoverable under substantially milder activation conditions than those required by the investigated conventional zeolites. This work not only provides a high‑performance material for selective dehydration, but also establishes a bioinspired adaptive adsorption mechanism for designing water‐selective adsorbents.

paper.title: Site-Selective Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics and Its Integration with Replica-Exchange Methods
paper.abstract: We developed site-selective Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (ssGaMD), which selectively enhances molecular motions associated with a specified region or set of interactions. The method allows selected dihedral, electrostatic, and Lennard–Jones energy terms to be biased independently or in combination, while limiting direct biasing of the rest of the system. ssGaMD can be combined with replica-exchange umbrella sampling (ssGaREUS) or temperature replicaexchange molecular dynamics (ssGaREMD) to further enhance the sampling of association and dissociation processes and conformational changes. We implemented these methods in the GENESIS MD simulation software and applied them to aspirin binding to β-cyclodextrin, PP1 binding to Src kinase, and Trp-cage folding. Selectively boosting interactions involved in binding efficiently promoted molecular association and dissociation, while combining ssGaMD with replica-exchange methods accelerated the convergence of binding and folding free-energy landscapes. These methods offer a flexible approach to studying ligand binding and other biomolecular processes in which slow dynamics are governed by specific local interactions.

paper.title: Dynamics and Structure of Room Temperature Ionic Liquids: Ultrafast IR Experiments and MD Simulations of the Ion Cage Model
paper.abstract: Abstract Dynamics in room-temperature ionic liquids (ILs) and the solvation of charged and neutral molecules are important to applications of ILs in battery technology, organic synthesis, and many other areas. Using ultrafast IR spectroscopy, pulse-field-gradient (pfg) NMR, and MD simulations, we investigated three ionic liquids that share the same cation but differ in their anions. IR polarization-selective pump-probe and 2D IR experiments were performed on a negatively charged probe, thiocyanate, to investigate IL dynamics. It was found that thiocyanate is an excellent surrogate for the IL anions. We employed a neutral probe, methylthiocyanate, to determine how a neutral solute’s dynamics and interactions differ from those of the RTIL ions. The pfg-NMR experiments, performed on all liquids and species, measured the translational diffusion constants. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations were performed to understand the experimental observables within the IL cage model, in which cations surround an anion (anion cage), and anions surround a cation (cation cage) for all ionic species, including the ionic probe. The neutral probe is surrounded by a combination of cations and anions (neutral probe cage). The cage model shows that the dynamical properties, including translational diffusion, orientational diffusion, and viscosity, are determined by the cage escape time, te, i.e., the time for an ion to leave the group of ions surrounding an ion of the opposite charge or the neutral probe. It is observed that te is correlated with the slowest component of the cage structural fluctuations measured by 2D IR.

paper.title: Geometrical Constraints Weaken a Nickel–Hydrogen Bond and Enable the Homolytic H2 Evolution Mechanism
paper.abstract: Mechanistic studies of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) are helping advance catalysis towards energy storage technologies based on water splitting. Homolytic H–H bondforming pathways are one of the fundamental mechanisms of HER, yet well-defined examples of bimetallic coupling in molecular HER catalysts remain extremely rare. A planar tetradentate bipyridine diphosphinite ligand (PONNOP) is reported that constrains the geometry of nickel complexes, weakening the Ni–H bond dissociation free energy and enabling H2 evolution via the homolytic pathway. Crystallography, magnetism, absorption spectroscopy, and computational studies provide insight into the electronic structure enforced by the rigid tetradentate PONNOP ligand, which results in a very weak Ni–H bond in a transiently formed metal hydride. Cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry studies are consistent with electrocatalytic HER via the homolytic mechanism. The ability of a tetradentate ligand to induce M–H bond-weakening is discussed as a possible design element in HER by Earth-abundant catalysts.

paper.title: Dynamic ZrO x Clusters Enhanced Redox Couple and ─CHO/OH − Co‐Adsorption for Efficient Electrooxidation of Alcohols/Aldehydes
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The electrochemical oxidation of biomass‐derived alcohols and aldehydes to produce high‐value carboxylic acids is a more sustainable strategy for achieving biomass upgrading. However, traditional metal oxyhydroxide (MOOH) catalysts suffer from inefficient M 2+ /M δ+ (δ≥ 3) cycling. Herein, we report a novel ZrO x ─MOOH interfacial synergy in electrocatalytic reaction, achieved by modifying traditional MOOH materials with ZrO x as a dynamic electronic regulator for efficient oxidation of alcohols and aldehydes. The ZrO 2 clusters are reduced to lower‐valent suboxides (ZrO x ) during the Ni 2+ →Ni 3+ process. The formed ZrO x enhances the adsorption of the 5‐hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) (aldehyde C─O) and OH − , and enables faster charge transfer with more NiOOH species participating in the Ni 2+ /Ni 3+ redox by modulating the charge density on Ni. The ZrO x ─NiOOH‐catalyzed HER//HMFOR process achieves stable 2,5‐furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) yield and Faradaic efficiency (>95%) over 24 consecutive electrolytic cycles. When applied to a flowing HMFOR system (∼1 A/cm 2 , 1.50 V, 200 mM), the overall FDCA yield reaches 90%. Technical‐economic analysis (TEA) demonstrates the economic viability of the system. This work reveals biphasic evolution behavior of catalyst interface, providing a new design paradigm for electrocatalysts in the efficient upgrading of alcohols and aldehydes.

paper.abstract: A catalyst- and fluoride-free electrochemical method for the use of readily available thioethers as alkyl donors in C-O and C-N bond formation to furnish ethers, esters, and N-alkylated products is reported. The protocol exhibits broad functional group tolerance and is compatible with structurally complex substrates. Cyclic voltammetry studies rationalize the distinct behaviour of oxygen and nitrogen nucleophiles and guide the optimization of the electrochemical conditions, enabling the formation of coupled products from starting materials with both matched and mismatched redox potentials.

paper.title: Information Dynamics Explains Chemical Reactions: A Unified Framework from NaI Photodissociation to H2 Formation
paper.abstract: Chemical reactions are fundamentally the motion of atomic nuclei on potential energy surfaces. However, there is a methodological gap between quantum chemistry calculations and dynamical simulations: constructing potential energy surfaces is complicated, non-adiabatic couplings are difficult to treat, and different reaction types lack a unified language. In this work we introduce the information dynamics framework, reformulating chemical reactions as a three-element system: virtual space (potential energy surface rules), real space (initial wave packet data), and coupling matrix (projection mechanism). The virtual space defines the absolutely allowed region for nuclear motion, the real space provides the observed distribution of initial positions and momenta, and the coupling matrix drives the system toward a steady-state product according to the virtual space topology (gradient flow for a single surface or Landau-Zener transitions for two crossing surfaces). We validate the framework with three classic reactions: (1) NaI photodissociation (nonadiabatic, two crossing surfaces)—simulated dissociation yield 65.3% ± 1.5%, matching Zewail’s femtochemistry experiment (65%); (2) Cl2 photodissociation (adiabatic, single repulsive surface)dissociation yield 100%, mean relative kinetic energy 3.84 eV, in agreement with literature values;

paper.title: Unveiling Lithium-Atom Insertion and Clustering in Superionic Solid-State Electrolytes via Mechanical Deformation
paper.abstract: Abstract Solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are pivotal for next-generation energy systems, offering enhanced safety and higher energy density. In particular, a fundamental challenge in garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) and lithium superionic conductor Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS) applications is understanding and controlling the mechanical behavior at interfaces and under operational stresses, which can induce microcracking, void formation, and lithium dendrite growth. To address this gap, we employ machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with near-DFT accuracy and perform large-scale MD simulations to investigate two critical aspects: (1) the mechanical deformation of bulk LLZO under uniaxial compression and tension, revealing atomic-level mechanisms of elastic and plastic deformation, crack initiation, and failure; and (2) the kinetics of prescribed Li-atom insertion at model interfaces, exploring nucleation, clustering, and interface dynamics. Specifically, we identify two distinct lithium diffusion mechanisms: lithium ions in LGPS migrate via stepwise hopping along one-dimensional channels; in contrast, LLZO exhibits cooperative crowding (or “pushing”) within a three-dimensional network, where ion migration involves collective displacements and local structural distortions. These studies provide novel atomistic insights into the mechanical stability of SSEs under stress and the interfacial processes governing Li-atom insertion and clustering, contributing to the understanding and mitigation of key failure mechanisms in solid-state batteries.

paper.title: Directional Electric Fields at Designed MOF Sites: Implications for Electrostatic Preorganization and Catalysis
paper.abstract: Enzymes achieve their enormous catalytic power in part through electrostatic preorganization: non-covalent interactions arrange an electric field that is preorganized to stabilize the change in dipole moment between a reaction's ground and transition states. Thus, the catalytic relevance of an electric field depends not only on its magnitude but also on its orientation. Here we use the enforced rigidity of a metal–organic framework (MOF), PCN-521, to demonstrate this orientation dependence directly. We introduce an aldehyde carbonyl vibrational Stark probe in situ, first as a protected ketal, then deprotect it to reveal a carbonyl at the same node-capping site as a previously reported nitrile probe, extending field measurements to a field reporter of greater relevance to enzymatic catalysis. Electric field- vibrational frequency calibrated probes using the vibrational Stark effect report a trifluoroacetate field donor that projects nearly its full destabilizing field onto the collinear nitrile (sp, C≡N) but only a fraction onto the off-axis aldehyde (sp2, C=O) — a geometric effect. Because the framework's non-covalent contacts, unlike an enzyme active site's, cannot reorganize, this controlled, single-site comparison isolates alignment from magnitude. While electric fields are often invoked to explain observations near electrodes or droplet interfaces, these results show the importance of alignment which is often neglected.

paper.title: Preparation and Electrochemical Performance of N,S,F Co-Doped Porous Carbon Derived from FCC Slurry via Synergistic Doping and Pore Regulation for High-Performance Supercapacitors
paper.abstract: Abstract Utilizing fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) slurry as a carbon precursor represents a promising approach for the high-value conversion of industrial by-products, yet its application is restricted by inorganic impurities, limited pore accessibility, and insufficient active sites. In this work, a synergistic strategy combining ammonium sulfate-assisted in-situ N,S co-doping, KOH activation, and lithium fluoride–hydrochloric acid etching is developed to fabricate high-performance porous carbon. The incorporation of (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 enables simultaneous pore formation and heteroatom doping, while KOH activation constructs a hierarchical porous structure with enhanced surface area and ion transport pathways. Meanwhile, LiF–HCl etching effectively removes residual inorganic species and introduces fluorine functionalities, thereby modulating surface chemistry and pore architecture. Comprehensive structural analysis confirms the formation of a defect-rich carbon framework with uniformly distributed N, S, and F heteroatoms. The optimized sample (CNK-2) exhibits a high specific surface area of 2847 m 2 g -1 and a well-developed pore structure. Electrochemical measurements reveal a high specific capacitance of 401 F g -1 at 1 A g -1 with excellent rate capability and 87% capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles. These results highlight the synergistic effects of hierarchical porosity and multi-heteroatom doping, demonstrating significant potential for advanced supercapacitor applications.

paper.title: Chaotic dynamics and control in a resonance-mediated acoustic droplet vaporization model
paper.abstract: Abstract Acoustic droplet vaporization (ADV) is increasingly used in biomedical research, yet whether its underlying liquid-droplet dynamics under high driving pressure can become chaotic remains unresolved. Such complex dynamics could impair predictable activation and control of imaging and therapeutic responses. Here, we report, to our knowledge, the first evidence of deterministic chaotic dynamics in a liquid-droplet model of resonance-mediated ADV and demonstrate their control by using a weak second harmonic force. An irregular phase portrait, a broadband spectrum, and a positive Lyapunov exponent indicate chaos, and the bifurcation diagram traces the route from period-doubling to chaos. Furthermore, a second harmonic force with 4% of the primary pressure amplitude is applied to reconstruct a period-eight orbit by controlling chaos. Switching the second harmonic force on and off resolves the approach to recurrence and the control of chaotic motion. These results extend ADV resonance theory from amplification to chaotic dynamics and identify chaos control with little loss of radial excursion. The liquid-state droplet model predicts that chaos control can improve the harmonic ADV activation for nonlinear acoustic applications.

paper.title: Electrochemical Reduction of Acetonitrile to Gaseous C2 Products and Implications for Small Molecule Transformations
paper.abstract: Acetonitrile (CH3CN) is a polar aprotic solvent that is widely used in electrochemistry due to its large dielectric constant, strong ability to solubilize numerous substrates and catalysts, and stability under a wide range of applied potentials. In the context of electrocatalysis, reaction rates and product selectivities can differ markedly in CH3CN relative to other solvents, but the possibility of solvent reduction remains poorly explored. Herein, we report that CH3CN is reduced electrochemically in the presence of organic acids to form ethylene, ethane, ethylamine and ammonia. To our knowledge, this study constitutes the first report of electrochemical acetonitrile reduction to ethylene and the first molecular system to generate ethane. These reactions are catalyzed by iron tetraphenylporphyrins but also occur on plain glassy carbon electrodes, highlighting the generality of this reduction to a variety of other catalyst systems. Isotopic labelling coupled with high‐resolution gas chromatography-mass spectrometry shows that CH3CN is the source of ethylene and ethane and offers insights into plausible mechanistic pathways. Because the observed hydrocarbons and amines are also desired products of CO2 or N2 reduction or C‒N coupling reactions, these observations motivate increased scrutiny as to the origin of unusual reduction products when electrocatalytic reactions are performed in CH3CN.

paper.title: A neural operator framework for data-driven discovery of stability and receptivity in physical systems
paper.abstract: Understanding how complex systems respond to perturbations, such as whether they will remain stable or what their most sensitive patterns are, is a fundamental challenge across science and engineering. Traditional stability and receptivity (resolvent) analyses are powerful but rely on known equations and linearization, limiting their use in nonlinear or poorly modeled systems. Here, we introduce a data-driven framework that automatically identifies stability properties of both equilibrium points and periodic orbits, as well as optimal forcing responses from observation data alone, without requiring governing equations. By training a neural network as a dynamics emulator and using automatic differentiation to extract its Jacobian, we can perform stability and receptivity analyses directly from data. We demonstrate the method on systems of increasing complexity, from canonical models to high-dimensional fluid flows and a real-world climate dataset, employing model reduction where needed and successfully identifying dominant instability modes and optimal input–output structures, even in strongly nonlinear regimes. By leveraging a neural network emulator, we readily obtain a nonlinear representation of system dynamics while additionally retrieving intricate dynamical patterns that were previously difficult to resolve. This equation-free methodology establishes a broadly applicable tool for analyzing complex, high-dimensional datasets, with potential relevance to grand challenges in fields such as climate science, neuroscience, and fluid engineering.

paper.title: A systematic investigation of molecular encoding methods for drug property predictions across neural network and Transformer encoder-based model
paper.abstract: Abstract Fundamental investigations into how different molecular encoding methods affect molecular property prediction remain relatively limited. In this study, we extensively examined the optimal molecular encoding methods for molecular properties prediction using two prevalent structure designs: neural network model (MLP) and a Transformer encoder-based model (MLP + TL). For molecular encoding methods, we investigated several types of fingerprints, including traditional topological fingerprints, substructure-based fingerprints, and string-based representations. These two models were trained on seven well-known molecular datasets to evaluate different input molecular encoding methods based on evaluation metrics. On several biologically relevant classification tasks, including toxicity, mutagenicity, and side-effect prediction, our models consistently achieved average AUC values above 0.9. Beyond model performance, we further explored whether the Transformer encoder-based framework could provide interpretable insight. Rather than relying on external post-hoc explanation methods such as the local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) or the Deep SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we leveraged the model’s intrinsic attention weights as an internal interpretability signal for identifying potentially important feature. To further support this analysis, we conducted case studies on the BBBP and MUTAG datasets. The MLP + TL model using MACCS and PubChem as input can capture chemically interpretable groups that determined the major blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability and mutagenicity in Salmonella typhimurium . In particular, a comparison between Morphine and Heroin highlighted the role of hydroxyl-related substructures in BBB permeability prediction, which was consistently reflected in the attention weights. Overall, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting effective molecular encoding methods and contribute to the development of interpretable molecular informatics approaches for drug discovery.

paper.title: Polymer-Linked Nanoparticle Networks Running on Heat Can Act as Computing Devices
paper.abstract: Abstract Developing physical neural network (PNN) hardwares is important to next-generation artificial intelligence systems. Phononic devices─using heat current to encode and process information─is one of the solutions to neuromorphic computing. In this work, we backmap an artificial neural network (ANN) into a PNN simulation model using polymer networked nanoparticles (PNNPs). Our atomistic simulation results demonstrate that the polymer-linked nanoparticle networks can potentially realize information processing─viz., classification of input temperatures according to the output heat currents. Using high-throughput molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and the trust region Bayesian optimization (TuRBO) methods, we tune the plasticity of polymer linkers and the temperatures of nanoparticles─28 parameters in total─to optimize the performance of the PNNP machines, which is analogous to tuning of the weights and bias of the corresponding ANNs. After five rounds of high-throughput MD simulations, we demonstrate that the PNNP machine can better label different input temperatures, and thus its performance is improved. We also use a testing data set to verify the heat flow outputs from the top five PNNP machines in each round.

paper.title: Bulk Boundary Condition for Semi-Infinite Surfaces in Density Functional Theory
paper.abstract: Abstract We present a bulk boundary condition formalism for semi-infinite surfaces in Kohn–Sham density functional theory. The approach exploits the nearsightedness of electronic interactions to confine the calculation to a localized surface region, where the electron density is evaluated via density matrix decay with bulk values of potential imposed in the interior, and the electrostatic potential is solved subject to bulk boundary conditions. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the formalism through representative calculations.

paper.title: Bimetallic Metal‐Acetylide Frameworks for Highly Selective and Durable H 2 O 2 Electrosynthesis
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Metal‐acetylide frameworks (MAFs) feature tunable d–π orbital hybridization between transition metal centers and π‐ conjugated acetylide linkers. Here we report a two‐dimensional (2D) MAF, ZnTTPP‐Ni‐AF, assembled from zinc‐thienylporphyrin units (ZnTTPP) and nickel(II)‐bis(acetylide) linkers (─C≡C─Ni(PBu 3 ) 2 ─C≡C─, Bu = ─CH 2 CH 2 CH 2 CH 3 ), as a selective electrocatalyst for the two‐electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e − ORR) to H 2 O 2 . In alkaline electrolyte, ZnTTPP‐Ni‐AF achieves 94% H 2 O 2 selectivity and >90% Faradaic efficiency (FE) in an H‐cell, with excellent stability over 148 h. In a flow cell, it maintains >91% FE from 20 to 160 mA cm −2 , delivering an H 2 O 2 yield rate of 13.68 mol g −1 h −1 at 160 mA cm −2 . Combined experimental and theoretical studies reveal that synergy between Zn−N 4 porphyrinic centers and Ni II ‐bis(acetylide) motifs promotes O 2 activation and stabilizes the *OOH intermediate, steering the ORR toward the 2e − pathway. Enhanced Ni‐3 and O‐2 p orbital hybridization facilitates proton‐coupled electron transfer to *OOH while suppressing O─O bond cleavage. This work demonstrates that engineering orbital hybridization and bimetallic cooperativity in MAFs provides an effective strategy to overcome the intrinsic activity‐selectivity trade‐off in electrocatalytic H 2 O 2 synthesis.

paper.title: Compartmentalized Microgels with Programmed Acoustic Anisotropy for Orthogonal Ultrasound-Triggered Motion and Cargo Release
paper.abstract: Compartmentalization is a fundamental organizational principle in nature, enabling anisotropy required for controlled locomotion and spatiotemporal regulation of biological processes. Inspired by this principle, we present a one-step strategy to fabricate compartmentalized anisotropic microgels via liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) in aqueous droplets. Upon sodium chloride addition, concentrated N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAAm) solutions spontaneously separate into NIPAAm-rich and NIPAAm-poor phases. Integrating this process into microfluidic droplets followed by photopolymerization enables continuous fabrication of anisotropic PNIPAAm microgels with two compartments of distinct stiffness. Synthetic and biological macromolecules can be selectively loaded into different compartments according to their polarity. Crucially, LLPS-generated acoustic contrast enables two independently addressable functionalities under biocompatible ultrasound (US). Lowfrequency, low-intensity US induces propulsion at speeds of approximately 10 microgel diameters per second without cargo release, whereas high-frequency, higher-intensity US at biocompatible settings selectively degrades one compartment, enabling on-demand cargo release. Complementary computer simulations further elucidate the physical mechanisms underlying acoustically driven motion. This work establishes LLPS-driven compartmentalization as a design principle for multifunctional colloidal microrobots with independently programmable propulsion and cargo release, opening new avenues for targeted drug delivery and soft robotics.

paper.title: Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence
paper.abstract: Abstract AI models are increasingly used in scientific discovery and human decision-making. Yet how AI models work and what risks they pose remain poorly understood. As AI development becomes faster and more automated, research on the mechanisms underlying AI remains largely manual, widening the gap between model capabilities and our ability to understand and control them. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mechanist, an agentic system that uses AI as a scientific instrument for the autonomous discovery of mechanisms underlying AI. To ground novel mechanism hypotheses, we construct a scientific knowledge graph of 13,000 studies on AI mechanisms, alongside a multidisciplinary database of 43 million papers spanning 26 fields. For reliable experiment execution, we curate a library of 32 foundational methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation. Compared with Claude Code and existing AI-scientist systems, Mechanist generates higher-quality mechanism hypotheses and executes experiments more reliably. Mechanist advances the mechanism science of AI from autonomously understanding how AI models work to controlling their behaviour. Specifically, Mechanist first uncovers a counterintuitive safety risk in scientific laboratories, showing that unsafe traits can transfer to fine-tuned student models through apparently safe training data and emerge across modalities. Mechanist then develops a mechanism theory of belief, revealing how models represent world knowledge, form beliefs, infer the beliefs of others, and how these mechanisms emerge during pretraining. Building on this mechanism theory of belief, Mechanist develops targeted interventions that improve model performance across diverse scenarios. Finally, Mechanist advances interdisciplinary discovery through mechanistic design, providing an alternative to the computationally intensive generate-and-rerank paradigm.

paper.title: RetroMol: Knowledge Distillation of Energy-Based Retrosynthesis Models
paper.abstract: Retrosynthesis prediction is a central task in computer-aided synthesis planning, and synthesizability remains a persistent bottleneck in AI-driven molecular and materials discovery. We introduce RetroMol, a family of compact text-based models that transfers an energy-based critic’s ranking of candidate reactant sets into the generator itself. RetroBase, an 11M-parameter transformer encoderdecoder trained on two-reactant USPTO reactions, achieves Top-1 and Top-5 accuracies of 46.8% and 67.8% on a held-out test split. RetroERM, an energybased model over molecular fingerprint counts, scores RetroBase’s candidates, and its ranking preferences are distilled back into the generator. The distilled model, RetroDistil, reaches 52.6% Top-1 and 73.5% Top-5 under identical data and evaluation, improving on RetroBase by 5.7–6.8 points at Top-1/3/5 with no reranking stage at inference and no increase in model size. Distilling a critic is therefore a practical way to improve a compact retrosynthesis generator without larger or more complicated architectures.

paper.title: Direct Sampling of Nuclear-Quantum Chemical Equilibria by Path-Integral Reaction Ensemble Monte Carlo
paper.abstract: Abstract Reaction ensemble Monte Carlo samples chemical composition directly but usually treats the explicit environment with classical nuclei, whereas path-integral methods represent nuclear quantum effects explicitly but generally infer reaction equilibria from partition-function or free-energy ratios between predefined states. We formulate path-integral reaction ensemble Monte Carlo (PI-RxMC), a reaction-constrained expanded ensemble that samples chemical sectors and nuclear paths jointly, and derive the Metropolis-Hastings rule for sector changes, including sector weights, normalization factors, proposal probabilities, coordinate transformations, and Jacobians; for fixed nuclei with changing bonding topology, the free-ring-polymer contribution cancels exactly. Independent finite-P analytical, bond-topology, and rovibrational benchmarks validate the method, and direct sector-population estimates for H2 + D2 ⇌ 2HD agree with independent quantum results from 200 to 700 K. A second benchmark, AB ⇌ A + B with Δν = +1, explicitly recovers the reaction-volume and 1 M standard-state factors and exhibits a nearly 3-fold nuclear-quantum enhancement of the equilibrium constant. A bead-level slit field further demonstrates coupling to an explicit environment.

paper.title: A symmetry-field theoretical framework for quasi-stationary interfaces in fully miscible fluids
paper.abstract: Long-lived sharp interfaces in fully miscible fluids exhibit a transient quartic excess free-energy landscape and a Fermi–Dirac logistic concentration profile, whose microscopic statistical-mechanical origin has remained unresolved. Here, we develop an independent statistical-mechanical theory based on a microscopic pair Hamiltonian and the corresponding grand partition function. Exchange symmetry naturally introduces the invariant p=c1−c, whose regular local expansion uniquely generates the quartic excess free-energy density as the leading nonvanishing contribution after coarse-graining the microscopic Hamiltonian. The resulting free-energy functional completely determines the Euler–Lagrange equation of the quasi-stationary interface, whose exact solution is the Fermi–Dirac logistic profile. The independently derived microscopic formulation converges to the same quartic free-energy functional obtained previously from a continuum variational approach, thereby establishing a unified microscopic statistical-mechanical framework for quasi-stationary interfaces.

paper.title: Hybrid modeling for improved structure prediction of large protein complexes
paper.abstract: An automated framework, HDOCK-Multimer (HDM), is developed that integrates ab initio docking and combinatorial assembly for the structure prediction of large protein complexes. paper.title: Systematically Constructing QM regions for Calculating QM/MM Absorption Spectra
paper.abstract: Hybrid simulations utilizing both quantum mechanics and molecular mechanics (QM/MM) are widely used to model complex problems, such as the electronic excitation of chromophores embedded in a protein environment. Its success requires a careful choice of the portion of the system to include in the QM region to obtain accurate results. Chemical intuition and/or proximity arguments are often used to select the QM region for excited state calculations aiming to compute absorption spectra, but such choices do not guarantee accuracy. We compare four schemes for selecting the minimal set of protein residues that must be treated quantum mechanically to reproduce a reference spectrum: distance analysis, charge shift analysis, point charge variation analysis, and subtractive analysis. Charge shift analysis is the most robust: in both systems studied it identifies the smallest QM region that reproduces the reference spectral shape and absorption maximum, at moderate computational cost, using a threshold that transfers between systems. Because the resulting regions are both accurate and minimal, converged excited state calculations become affordable at scale, laying a foundation for large, internally consistent datasets of excited state properties in extended systems. We release an open-source implementation that automates the full workflow, including residue selection and determination of the QM/MM boundary, so a converged QM region can be built for a new system without manual intervention.
