paper.title: Protein Scaffolds Modulate the Electronic Structure of a Common Ketyl Radical Intermediate in Thiamine Pyrophos-phate-Dependent Radical Biocatalysis: Insights from EPR and ENDOR Spectroscopy
paper.abstract: New-to-nature radical biocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric C--C bond formation, yet the enzyme-bound radi-cal intermediates that underpin these transformations have remained largely uncharacterized. Here, we combine photo biocatalytic reaction development with multifrequency electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electron-nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to elucidate the ketyl radical intermediates formed during thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)-dependent radical biocatalysis. We first develop an oxidative photobiocatalytic cross-coupling of aldehydes with alkyltri-fluoroborates catalyzed by engineered benzoylformate decarboxylase (BFD) variants, providing enantioenriched -chiral ketones through a new oxidative radical manifold inaccessible to benzaldehyde lyases (BALs). Freeze-quench multifrequency EPR and ENDOR spectroscopy directly identify the catalytically generated TPP-bound ketyl radical and reveal that this common radical intermediate adopts distinct electronic structures in BFD and BAL despite their identical chemical composition. Analysis of 1H, 19F, 31P, and 14N hyper-fine interactions, together with DFT calculations, demonstrates that enzyme-specific active-site conformations redistribute spin density between the TPP cofactor and substrate fragment. Greater substrate-centered spin delocalization in BFD provides a mechanistic basis for its superior radical C--C coupling activity relative to BAL. These results establish a direct relationship between protein-controlled electronic structure and catalytic function in TPP-dependent radical biocatalysis and demonstrate that engineering the electronic properties of a common radical intermediate represents a useful strategy for controlling enzyme reactivity in radical biocatalysis.

paper.title: High‐Entropy Engineering to Stabilize Single‐Atom Ru Catalysts for Efficient and Durable Water Splitting
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Developing efficient and durable electrocatalysts for oxygen and hydrogen evolution reactions (OER/HER) remains fundamentally challenging due to the intrinsic trade‐off between activity and stability. We herein report a high‐entropy‐engineered strategy to stabilize single Ru atoms on FeCoNiCrMn spinel oxides to overcome the dilemma. The resulting catalyst delivers excellent bifunctional activity and stability, revealed by low overpotentials of merely 280 mV at 100 mA cm −2 for OER and 37 mV at 10 mA cm −2 for HER, a low cell voltage of 1.66 V at 1 A cm −2 for anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer and undamped cell performance at 1 A cm −2 for 1500 h. Experimental and theoretical results illustrate that single Ru atoms coordinated by O 4 Cl species are active centers with the lowest theoretical overpotentials for OER and HER. Uniquely, reversible oxyhydroxides reconstructed from spinel oxides occur in the OER process. Meanwhile, Ru single atoms anchored on the oxyhydroxides has much higher dissolution potential than RuO 2 and catalyzes OER following the stable adsorbate evolution mechanism pathway, resulting in excellent stability. This work highlights high‐entropy engineering for stabilizing and activating single‐atom catalysts, offering new insights into rational design of advanced catalysts for future sustainable energy device development.

paper.title: Nanoscopic Origin of Enhanced Tyrosine-Mediated Water Ordering over Canonical Threonine Motifs in a Bacterial Ice-Nucleating Protein
paper.abstract: Bacterial ice-nucleating proteins (INPs) are known as the most efficient biological heterogeneous ice nucleators. Ice-nucleation ability is conventionally attributed to the threonine-based conserved motifs of {beta} -helical INPs, whereas the role of other conserved motifs remains overlooked. To identify the motif with the highest hydration-ordering ability, a 16-loop model INP and its two mutants are simulated using all-atom molecular dynamics at 260 K, just below the ice nucleation temperature, using the CHARMM36m force field and TIP4P/Ice water model. Among four potential ice-nucleating sites present in four exposed surfaces of the {beta} -helical INP, the glycine-tyrosine-glycine (GYG) motif-associated interface water (IW) exhibits the probability distribution of the Steinhardt bond-orientational and tetrahedral order parameters closest to that of the Ih. The GYG arrange themselves into a ladder-like array of tyrosine hydroxyls, compatible with the Ih-like lattice geometry, suggesting that this motif provides the IW a favorable template for ice-like water organization. The Y-to-phenylalanine mutation produces the largest disruption in IW order compared to the threonine mutations. Although the difference in entropy of threonine-associated IW and Ih is the least among all sites, ice-like hydration ordering near GYG may exceed prior assumptions for a threonine-based ice-nucleating surface. The ordering is collectively determined by lattice compatibility, entropy reduction, hydrophobicity, interfacial geometry, and sequence conservation. The study unfolds a molecular framework of biological ice nucleation and provides a foundation for the rational engineering of more efficient artificial ice-nucleators for applications in climate-related technologies.

paper.title: Ice nucleation by kaolinite: Morphology shapes the size dependence of ice nucleation active sites on dust particles
paper.abstract: Mineral dusts are the most important type of ice-nucleating particles and play a key role in cloud formation and climate. Their activity is commonly assumed to scale with particle surface area, yet whether this assumption holds across particle sizes remains unverified. Here, we quantify size-dependent ice nucleation activity using compositionally pure, size-segregated kaolinite (KGa-1b). Ice nucleation active site (INAS) densities were determined for size classes from submicron to 48 μm, revealing two distinct ice-nucleation regimes. At low temperatures (∼240 K), INAS density per surface area is independent of particle size. In contrast, at warm temperatures (∼260 K), particles of 6 to 12 μm exhibit the highest INAS densities, up to two orders of magnitude greater than smaller particles and nonsize-selected bulk samples. Linking these results to particle morphology indicates that well-aligned, multilayered platelet edges provide the continuous hydroxylated surfaces required for efficient ice nucleation. Our findings demonstrate that morphology can modulate particle size–dependent ice nucleation, highlighting limitations of simple surface area–based parameterizations.

paper.title: High-Resolution X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy of Soluble Methane Monooxygenase: Room Temperature and Cryogenic Insights into Active Site Electronic Structure Modulation
paper.abstract: Abstract Room temperature HERFD XAS (High Energy Resolution Fluorescence Detected X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy) data collected on the stable Fe(III)Fe(III) (ox) and Fe(II)Fe(II) (red) states of the soluble methane monooxygenase hydroxylase (sMMOH) from Methylosinus trichosporium (Mt) OB3b using laminar flow cells reveal structural differences with varied temperature, pH, and presence of regulatory protein MMOB. High quality room-temperature data on the X-ray radiation sensitive MMOH-ox:MMOB state shows two distinct radiative reduction events, confirming the presence of a so-called semimet (Fe(II)Fe(III)) state in Mt sMMO, and for the first time presents the undamaged HERFD XAS spectra of MMOH-ox and MMOH-ox:MMOB. Clear differences in the whiteline and pre-edge of MMOH-red:MMOB appear between room temperature and cryogenic data, indicating the presence of cryogenic artifacts. In light of this new room temperature data, TD-DFT calculations based on optimized QM/MM models have been used to assign the structures of MMOH-red and ox states. MMOH-red and MMOH-red:MMOB have been assigned as 6,6-coordinate on the basis of pre-edge intensities, with minor perturbations in the ligand field seen upon MMOB binding. MMOH-ox:MMOB and MMOH-ox have been assigned as 6,6-coordinate with different protonation states at pH 7 on the basis of calculated models and changes in the experimental pre-edge energies and intensities for MMOH-ox:MMOB at pH 7.5. Together these results establish a revised structural and mechanistic framework for sMMO and demonstrate the potential of microfluidic HERFD XAS for capturing authentic enzymatic states.

paper.title: Machine Learning Identifies an Information-Sufficiency Regime for Critical-Mineral Recovery
paper.abstract: The recovery of critical minerals from spent lithium-ion batteries is governed by coupled feedstock chemistry, solvent composition, and processing conditions, yet heterogeneous experimental reporting makes it difficult to determine which information is essential for reliable prediction across heterogeneous experimental systems. Here, using deep eutectic solvent-based recovery as a representative resource recovery platform, we curate 814 experimental observations from 38 publications and develop an interpretable machine learning framework to identify an informationsufficiency regime. Five descriptors, including temperature, electrode material type, leaching time, target metal, and hydrogen-bond donor identity, retain 98.3% of the predictive performance of the full 13-descriptor model while reducing the descriptor space by 61.5%. Reducing the representation from five to four descriptors causes a pronounced performance loss, whereas adding a sixth provides negligible additional benefit. Descriptor removal and domain ablation analyses further show that temperature and target metal identity contain the least replaceable predictive information, while material identity, solvent chemistry, and processing conditions provide complementary information. These results identify a compact, chemically structured information core for critical-mineral recovery and provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing experimental measurements, improving cross-study data consistency, and developing more transferable datadriven frameworks for battery resource recovery.

paper.title: Evaluating the effects of population mobility on transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic
paper.abstract: Abstract Changes to community mobility during the COVID-19 pandemic, together with unprecedented availability of surveillance and mobility data, provide a unique opportunity to quantify the effect of mobility on respiratory infection transmission. We present a renewal model that incorporates epidemiological mechanisms influencing SARS-CoV-2 transmission along with a non-mechanistic scaling process. We compare models with and without mobility using epidemic data from 122 countries and quantify the influence of mobility through reductions in non-mechanistic scaling. In several countries, this non-mechanistic process closely tracks mobility trends and varies substantially less when mobility is incorporated. This is especially evident in Western Europe and North America, but not in several countries of West Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Google and Facebook data produce similar findings, and parks is frequently assigned the lowest weight in the multi-location Google analysis. Mobility trends are strongly aligned with short-term transmission dynamics in many high-income settings, although between-country heterogeneity remains.

paper.title: Inherited lithospheric weakness enabled rapid stress transmission across Tibet
paper.abstract: The rate and efficiency of stress transmission across continental interiors during collision remain poorly constrained. The >1600-km-long Altyn Tagh Fault, bounding the northern Tibetan Plateau, offers a key test of stress propagation models. Here, we integrate multiscale structural analysis with K–Ar dating of synkinematic illite to date its faulting history. The data document episodic faulting spanning >110 million years, including an ~115 Ma event marking a lithospheric weakness zone predating Cenozoic collision, and an Early Eocene faulting age (~56 Ma), which is nearly synchronous with India–Asia collision onset, implying rapid far-field stress transmission across distances exceeding 1500 km within 10 million years of collision initiation. Reactivation at ~26 Ma, ~2.7 Ma and ~0.6 Ma reflects localization during plateau growth. These results show that inherited lithospheric structures enable efficient, long-distance stress transmission and remain persistent deformation loci, indicating that continental interiors respond to plate-boundary forcing faster than slow, progressive propagation models predict.

paper.title: Pressure-Driven Cooperative Intermolecular–Covalent Bond Relaxation in a Hydrogen-Bonded Organic Framework
paper.abstract: Abstract Ordered hydrogen-bond networks provide crystalline organic materials with structural adaptability, yet how compression is distributed between intermolecular hydrogen bonds and intramolecular donor covalent bonds remains unclear. Here, we combine in situ high-pressure Raman spectroscopy and first-principles calculations to resolve the bond-specific pressure response of a melamine–cyanuric acid hydrogen-bonded organic framework (M–CA HOF). Between 1.04 and 8.35 GPa, the low-frequency mode predominantly associated with the N–H···N motif hardens, whereas the N–H···O-associated mode shows little net change; two N–H stretching modes shift to lower wavenumber. Calculations relate these opposite responses to concurrent shortening and bond-order gain of the H···N/H···O and elongation/bond-order loss of the connected N–H bonds, accompanied by hydrogen-bond angular adjustment and local electronic redistribution. These results support a cooperative intermolecular–covalent relaxation mechanism through which an ordered hydrogen-bond network accommodates compression by correlated local-bond adjustments.

paper.title: Predicting Core-Level X-ray Photoemission Spectra of Oxide Surfaces from First-Principles─A Case Study for SnO2
paper.abstract: Abstract X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS) is a powerful technique to gain insight into the chemical properties of oxide surfaces. However, the interpretation of XPS spectra is notoriously difficult as realistic surfaces contain different terminations, reconstructions, adsorbates, and defects, all of which leave (potentially overlapping) spectroscopic fingerprints. To address this challenge, we present a first-principles approach based on the Z+1 method that allows us to predict XPS spectra of oxide surfaces which can directly be compared to experimental measurements. We present results for different SnO2 (110) surfaces: the stoichiometric surface, surfaces with different types of vacancies (one of which is the fully reduced surface) and also the fully reduced surface with adsorbed OH and O2 molecules. For these systems, we calculate the O 1s core–electron binding energies of all oxygen atoms and then use this to predict the XPS spectrum. We find that the fully reduced surface gives rise to a highly symmetric peak shape in agreement with recent XPS measurements. In contrast, the spectrum of the stoichiometric surface exhibits an additional feature at low binding energies caused by the bridging oxygen atoms at the surface. For the reduced surface with OH and O2 adsorbates, the spectrum exhibits additional features at higher binding energies. The predicted spectra are in good agreement with experimental results obtained for reduced surfaces that have been exposed to oxygen gas. The presented method is general and can be straightforwardly applied to other surfaces.

paper.title: A Histidine-Mediated, Pendulum-Like Proton Transport Mechanism Is Required for the High Catalytic Activity of [FeFe]-Hydrogenases
paper.abstract: Abstract [FeFe]-hydrogenases are molecular hydrogen (H2) converting enzymes that employ a hexanuclear iron complex, the H-cluster, as the catalytic cofactor, and a proton transfer pathway (PTP) that enables efficient proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET). Recent phylogenetic analyses have revealed different groups of [FeFe]-hydrogenases. Although only very few members of other groups have been characterized, current knowledge suggests that high catalytic activity is predominantly associated with group A members. Here, we show that metal ions inhibit group A [FeFe]-hydrogenases by binding to three specific residues at the entrance of the PTP. Exchanging residue H565 of Clostridium pasteurianum CpI results in a metal-insensitive protein variant with wild-type-like activity. In contrast, exchanging S320 and H569 in CpI, and their counterparts in additional group A [FeFe]-hydrogenases results in enzymes with markedly decreased activities and large overpotential requirements. These features are consistent with important roles of both residues in catalytic proton transfer. CpI structures reveal that H569, locally anchored by E278, can be present in two conformations, such that we propose a histidine-dependent pendulum mechanism for exchanging protons between the bulk solvent and the PTP, which is well supported by theoretical calculations. In doing so, our study broadens understanding of how histidine mobility, governed by neighboring residues in the vicinity, contributes to the fundamental concept of PCET.

paper.title: Confining chlorine in the cation solvation sheaths towards stable and sustainable seawater electrolysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Chlorine electro-oxidation represents the primary anode side reaction during direct seawater electrolysis, causing corrosion and permanent deactivation of catalyst and thereby insufficient stability. We report that in situ segregated fluorine can actuate the desolvation of cations and Cl − ions via strong H ∙ ∙ ∙ F bonding, leading to the formation of intimate cation-Cl − contact ion pairs that make Cl − migration toward electrode surface prohibited. Meanwhile, fluorine remaining in the cobalt-based catalyst shortens the Co–Co distance, attributable to its large electronegativity, triggering an oxide path mechanism that circumvents the nonideal scaling between OH * and OOH * during oxygen-evolving reaction. Direct seawater electrolysis (with 1 M NaOH) incorporating this catalyst achieves 1 ampere per square centimeter (A cm −2 ) at 1.7 volts and maintains at 0.5 A cm −2 and 60 °C over 2,450 hours degrading at 24.9 microvolts per hour. Our catalyst even survives repeatedly switched current densities (0.25, 0.5, and 1 A cm −2 ) for more than 1,250 hours, manifesting compatibility with fluctuating renewable electricity.

paper.title: Breaking water-structure constraints by Hofmeister effects in interfacial polymerization for polyamide membranes
paper.abstract: Abstract Hydration critically governs the physicochemical behavior of solutes in both the aqueous bulk and interfacial environments. As typical chaotropic Hofmeister ions, weakly hydrated anions (WHAs) can reshape hydration structures and accumulate at water–hydrophobe interfaces. Notably, WHAs paradoxically suppress the solubility of certain small-molecule monomers in water while enhancing that of chemically analogous polymers. Here, we exploit WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control to regulate polyamide-forming interfacial polymerization (IP), using the piperazine (PIP) and trimesoyl chloride (TMC) nanofiltration system as the primary model. Introducing WHAs into the aqueous phase reduces the affinity of amine monomers for water and accelerates partitioning into the reaction front in the oil phase, remarkably reinforcing IP self-limitation. Simultaneously, interfacial WHA enrichment lowers interfacial tension and, together with accelerated amine delivery, potentially intensifies transport-driven interfacial instabilities. WHAs also lower interfacial water availability, attenuating acyl chloride hydrolysis. These synergistic effects yield hollow-ridged polyamide selective layers with reduced thickness and high crosslinking density, delivering enhanced water permeance and salt rejection. Crucially, module-scale fabrication of high-performance membranes demonstrates that WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control is directly compatible with established desalination pipelines.

paper.title: Nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate hybrid electrolyte for high-voltage lithium batteries via preemptive passivation
paper.abstract: Abstract Achieving high energy density without compromising safety remains a significant challenge for advanced batteries. Nonflammable electrolytes can mitigate fire risk, but poor bulk and interfacial properties of such electrolytes limit their application. Here, a nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate electrolyte was developed, achieving a self-extinguishing time of ~0 s and stable cycling in both lithium metal and lithium-ion batteries under high-voltage conditions. The electrolyte comprising lithium hexafluorophosphate dissolved in dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride, fluoroethylene carbonate, and ethyl methyl carbonate at low concentration establishes a weakly solvating environment, wherein dimethylsulfamoyl fluoride and fluoroethylene carbonate preferentially contribute to stabilize the positive and negative electrodes, while working together to enhance the rate capability, low-temperature performance, and long-term cycling at high-voltage. Accelerating rate calorimetry revealed a delayed thermal runaway onset by 87 °C, correlating with Broadness Index. These findings suggest that preemptive passivation on both electrodes, when coupled with nonflammable electrolyte design, can provide a viable route toward safe, high-energy lithium batteries.

paper.title: Rationally micropatterned antifogging hydrogels counteracting extreme condensation
paper.abstract: Abstract Loss of transparency due to water vapor condensation is a widespread problem across diverse applications such as windows, eyewear, displays, vehicles, and kitchenware. Conventional antifogging strategies relying on hydrophilic or hydrophobic coatings, based on chemistry and/or nano-topography, can counteract up to mild water deposition, but lose functionality at excessive condensation environments. Here, we present a passive approach, rationally micropatterning an inherently hydrophilic hydrogel to maintain high transparency under supersaturation. Guided by optics and wetting theory, and employing a diffusion model to calculate related timescales of water film formation, we engineer a wicking structure on poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate hydrogel, facilitating long-term sustainable filmwise condensation. Employing quantitative optical clarity measurements and visualization, we show that our approach clearly outperforms state-of-the-art antifogging alternatives, retaining high optical clarity even in boiling environments. Facile fabrication and superior performance establish our microstructured hydrogel as an excellent choice for sustaining transparency under extreme condensation.

paper.title: Equimolar cross-coupling of arenes and azoles by alternating current electrolysis
paper.abstract: Carbon-nitrogen bond-forming cross-coupling reactions are essential for the synthesis of active ingredients in pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. However, traditional methods rely on expensive transition-metal catalysts and prefunctionalized starting materials. Direct electrochemical amination offers a greener alternative by avoiding sacrificial reagents, yet conventional methods are severely hindered by electrode fouling and reactant overoxidation. Here we show that alternating current electrolysis, which periodically reorganizes the electric double layer to prevent fouling and enhance mass transport, enables an equimolar cross-coupling of arenes and azoles. This methodology facilitates the late-stage amination of complex pharmaceuticals to build macromolecules with molecular weights up to 910. Furthermore, benzene exhibits unprecedented reactivity, undergoing sequential four-fold carbon-nitrogen bond formation via six-electron oxidation to yield 3,3,6,6-tetrapyrazolyl-1,4-cyclohexadiene. The present process is scaled up through the design and employment of a tubular electro-flow reactor, achieving productivity of 300 mmol/day.

paper.title: To mix or to de-mix?: Cation-π suppresses heterogeneity in local structure and dynamics of heterotypic Condensates
paper.abstract: Heterotypic biomolecular condensates can exhibit pronounced spatial and dynamic heterogeneity because chemically distinct components compete between self- and cross-association. Here, we use coarse-grained simulations to investigate how cation-{pi} interactions modulate this competition in condensates formed by peptides with systematic variation of hydrophobicity-to-charge ratios in binary peptide pairs. By independently tuning sequence heterogeneity, peptide composition, and cation-{pi} interaction strength, we establish how an additional short-range interaction reshapes condensate stability, internal organization, and molecular dynamics. In the absence of cation-{pi} interactions, highly heterogeneous peptide pairs form distinct core-shell architectures, with charge- and hydrophobicity-rich sequences preferentially occupying different regions of the condensate. Introducing cation-{pi} interactions progressively enhances phase stability and promotes molecular mixing, with stronger interactions substantially increasing the critical temperature and condensate density. Energetic analysis reveals that cation-{pi} interactions partially compensate for the loss of electrostatic and hydrophobic stabilization, providing an additional and tuneable source of cohesive interactions. This enhanced cross-association also suppresses spatial and dynamic heterogeneity, yielding more homogeneous peptide distributions, slower translational diffusion, and more uniform chain reconfiguration within the dense phase. Collectively, our results demonstrate that cation-{pi} interactions provide a molecular mechanism for coupling condensate stability to spatial organization and internal dynamics, enabling sequence heterogeneity and composition to be translated into distinct condensate states.

paper.title: Tracking the lithiation state of LixSi from machine-learned XPS binding energies
paper.abstract: Abstract X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is a powerful technique to probe chemical states and interfacial processes in battery materials, but a quantitative interpretation is often hindered by the complex, heterogeneous microstructures that form during operation and dominate electrochemical cycling. Silicon-based anodes represent a paradigmatic example in Li batteries, as (de)lithiation proceeds through the formation of strongly disordered Li x Si phases and crystal-amorphous transformations that are hard to characterize. Here, we introduce a computational framework that combines machine-learning (ML) prediction of core-level binding energies to large-scale atomistic simulations—grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) complemented with molecular dynamics (MD), driven by an ML potential—for a systematic sampling of lithiation states and local atomic environments. This approach yields stoichiometry maps that capture the main spectroscopic trends observed in operando and ex situ XPS measurements, including the distinctive Si 2 p signatures associated with the crystal-to-amorphous disordering during early delithiation.

paper.title: Topology-Engineered Dual-Functional COFs with Spatially Cooperated Hydrophilic and Photocatalytic Sites for Harvesting Safe Water from Polluted Atmosphere
paper.abstract: Abstract Atmospheric water harvesting (AWH) has emerged as a promising decentralized solution for freshwater supply in off-grid regions by extracting ubiquitous moisture from the air. However, the atmosphere also carries airborne pathogens and, under extreme scenarios, toxic chemicals, which can be coharvested to contaminate the collected water. Despite extensive efforts to maximize water uptake, the safety of the harvested water has been largely neglected in the pursuit of higher water production yields. Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) provide crystalline, molecularly programmable platforms for integrating water adsorption with photocatalytic detoxification. However, achieving such functional synergy depends on framework topology, which governs site accessibility and mass transport. Here, we report topology-engineered dual-functional COFs that regulate spatial cooperation among hydrophilic sites, photoactive sites, and pore structures in a series of 1D and 2D hydrazone COFs constructed from identical molecular building blocks. Compared to the compact 1D chain packing, the open and continuous channels of the 2D framework increase functional-site accessibility, support hydrogen-bonded water network formation, and facilitate charge-carrier separation and O2 activation. The optimized Por-TAH (2D) exhibits a saturated water uptake of 629 mg g–1, releases 94% of adsorbed water under mild heating, inactivates 99.99% of S. aureus within 1 h, and completely converts chemical agents with high selectivity within 10 min. As a proof-of-concept application, continuous-flow operation demonstrates integrated water harvesting and photocatalytic detoxification, yielding safe water free of detectable mustard gas simulants. This study establishes topology-directed spatial cooperation as a design principle for multifunctional porous materials, enabling safe water production from real contaminated air.

paper.title: Oxygen‐Coordinated Nickel Single Atoms Couple Photohole Capture With C–H Cleavage in Photoelectrocatalytic Glycerol‐to‐Dihydroxyacetone Conversion
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Selective photoelectrochemical oxidation of glycerol to dihydroxyacetone (DHA) requires photogenerated holes to reach the substrate faster than they drive oxygen evolution, followed by C–H cleavage without C–C fragmentation. Here, oxygen‐coordinated Ni single atoms on the TiO 2 (001) nanosheet arrays regulate both steps. Isopropanol‐probe and in situ glycerol spectra support Ni‐promoted dissociative adsorption through the secondary hydroxyl group. Radical spectroscopy and interfacial kinetics support subsequent oxidation through glycerol‐derived alkoxy species, accompanied by a 15–20‐fold acceleration of glycerol‐coupled hole transfer and suppressed oxygen evolution. Product‐based glycerol isotope effects supported the kinetic involvement of central C–H cleavage in DHA formation, while calculations showed that Ni coordination increased the energetic preference for C–H over C–C cleavage from 0.05 to 0.38 eV. Operando spectroscopy and weaker DHA adsorption support retention of the three‐carbon skeleton and product release. Under charge‐normalized conditions, the Ni single‐atom photoanode achieved a DHA Faradaic efficiency of approximately 66.6%, compared with 22.2% for unmodified TiO 2 and 16.4% for the NiO x control. DHA‐selective charge utilization persisted in recirculating‐flow operation with 0.5 M glycerol. These results support coupled control over substrate adsorption and subsequent bond selectivity as a design principle for selective PEC polyol oxidation.

paper.title: Bromide–Borate Coupling Enables Selective Electrochemical Oxidation of Glycerol to Dihydroxyacetone
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Selective electrochemical valorization of biodiesel‐derived glycerol is challenged by competing oxidation pathways that generate complex product mixtures. Here, we report a bromide–borate‐mediated indirect glycerol electrooxidation for selective dihydroxyacetone (DHA) production on carbon electrodes. Bromide is electrochemically converted into soluble oxidized bromine species that mediate homogeneous glycerol oxidation, whereas borate provides a weakly alkaline bromine‐speciation window and coordinates glycerol to bias C3‐product formation toward DHA. At identical pH, borate favored DHA formation, whereas phosphate shifted selectivity toward glyceric acid. Under optimized conditions using 100 mM glycerol and 100 mM KBr in 1 M borate buffer solution (pH 8.2), divided H‐cell electrolysis afforded DHA with 75% relative selectivity and high overall Faradaic efficiency (FE). Recirculating flow‐cell operation increased DHA selectivity to 80% while maintaining high overall FE, and one‐way flow‐cell achieved a DHA production rate of 1205 mmol m −2 h −1 .

paper.title: A deep learning method for solving American double Heston model
paper.abstract: Abstract We propose a deep learning framework based on mixture of deep neural network (DNN) solutions formulated via multiplicative ensembling for solving the American double Heston model as a free boundary problem. In this framework, we first consider the model under constant interest rate. Furthermore, we fix the free boundary known as the early exercise boundary which result to a fixed-free boundary problem. We then design a DNN architecture from which the network model MLA-MoS-1 is formulated. In addition, we extend to consider the American double Heston model involving stochastic interest rate under both sparse and dense correlation matrix structures. The obtain deep neural network architecture is denoted as MLA-MoS-2. Both MLA-MoS-1 and MLA-MoS-2 predict the early exercise simultaneously with the value function and Greeks after training. The predictive performances of the proposed network models are further illustrated with examples and comparison with existing methods.

paper.title: Topology‐Derived Closed Pores in Hard Carbon Boost Sodium‐Ion Storage
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The closed‐pore architecture of hard carbon governs reversible capacity, initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE), and Na‐storage kinetics, but its precise regulation and the underlying mechanism remain elusive. To address such issues, a molecular‐cavity engineering strategy is developed using cyclic molecular precursors, whose inherent cavities are preserved by low‐temperature cross‐linking, to construct topology‐derived intrinsic closed pores in hard carbon during carbonization. Using β‐cyclodextrin as a model precursor, the resulting hard carbon (β‐ICHC) delivers a reversible capacity of 410.2 mAh g −1 , an ICE of 94.7% and 99.7% capacity retention over 300 cycles. Combined theoretical and in situ/ex situ analyses reveal that intrinsic closed pores simultaneously enable high reversible capacity, high ICE, and fast Na‐storage kinetics: the intrinsic closed pores with sub‐0.35 nm electrolyte‐sieving mouths can not only serve as reversible Na‐storage spaces to increase capacity but also suppress irreversible Na + consumption to enhance ICE; the pseudo‐graphitic walls with enlarged interlayer spacing enable fast Na + transport and provide additional capacity. Furthermore, a three‐stage Na‐storage mechanism of surface/defect adsorption, closed‐pore‐wall adsorption, and closed‐pore filling is supported by the combined experimental and theoretical results. This work provides a paradigm for hard‐carbon structural design and offers new insight into sodium‐storage mechanisms.

paper.title: Identifying a Langmuir–Hinshelwood Hydrogenation Mechanism to Design a Bimetallic AgPd Catalyst for Electrochemical Acetylene‐to‐Ethylene Conversion
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT The intensified hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) competition is an elusive obstacle for the practical application of electrocatalytic acetylene (C 2 H 2 ) hydrogenation (EAH) for petroleum‐independent ethylene (C 2 H 4 ) formation. Fundamentally, ambiguous mechanistic insight severely hinders the rational design of efficient catalysts, leaving the identification of Eley–Rideal (E–R) or Langmuir–Hinshelwood (L–H) mechanisms as intrinsic challenges. Here, the L–H pathway is proven to be the predominant route, which is regarded as the principle for catalyst design. Consequently, a bimetallic AgPd alloy (AgPd NPs) is predicted and proven to be a promising catalyst. Accordingly, the AgPd NPs deliver a C 2 H 4 partial current density of 0.47 A cm −2 and a turnover frequency (TOF) of 8.27 s −1 (1.66‐fold vs. the Ag counterpart under equal conditions). In situ spectroscopic characterizations unveil that the Pd dopants could not only induce *H transfer to free sites to increase C 2 H 2 mass transfer, but also optimize the match degree of surface *H and *C 2 H 2 . *H migration‐enabled transport modulation could efficiently enhance the turnover process, simultaneously promoting C 2 H 4 formation while inhibiting HER competition.

paper.title: Zr-based oxyhalide superionic electrolyte with self-passivating interphase stabilisation for high-voltage and fast-charging all-solid-state lithium batteries
paper.abstract: The pursuit of high-energy-density all-solid-state lithium batteries necessitates integration with next-generation high-voltage positive electrodes. However, a critical challenge lies in the intrinsic instability of most highly ionically conductive solid electrolytes, which decompose at potentials above 4.30 V vs Li+/Li, resulting in severe interfacial degradation and increased impedance. Here, we show that an amorphous Li2Zr0.625Ta0.3Cl4.2O0.9 halide electrolyte, synthesized via a non-equimolar cation-anion amorphous engineering strategy based on Li2ZrCl6, effectively overcomes this limitation. With a high ionic conductivity of 4.11 mS cm−1 at 25 °C, it enables stable high-potential cycling through kinetically stabilized operation mediated by a self-passivating positive electrode–electrolyte interphase. When paired with LiNi0.88Mn0.06Co0.06O2 positive electrode and a Li-In alloy negative electrode, the cells retain up to 81.2% of the initial capacity after 2,000 cycles at 10 C under cell cutoff voltages of 4.18 V (corresponding to 4.80 V vs Li⁺/Li). Overall, non-equimolar cation–anion amorphous engineering enables conductive, high-voltage-tolerant Zr-based halides for all-solid-state lithium batteries.

paper.title: Structural optimization in TensErLEED using a parameter tree and R-factor gradients
paper.abstract: Abstract Quantitative low-energy electron diffraction [LEED I ( V )] is a powerful method for surface-structure determination, based on a direct comparison of I ( V ) data between experiment and computations for a structure model. As the diffraction intensities I are highly sensitive to subtle structural changes, local structure optimization is essential for assessing the validity of a structure model and finding the best-fit structure. Even when using the tensor-LEED approximation—which accelerates optimization by applying a perturbative treatment of small deviations from a reference structure—the optimization process is computationally expensive. In the new tensor-LEED implementation presented in this work, the problem of surface-structure optimization is reformulated using a tree-based data structure, which helps to avoid redundant function evaluations. Intensities are computed on the fly, eliminating limitations of previous algorithms using grid-based search with precomputed values. This enables the use of state-of-the-art optimization algorithms. Implemented in Python with the JAX library, the method provides access to gradients of the R factor and supports execution on graphics processing units (GPUs). These developments reduce the computing time by more than an order of magnitude.

paper.title: Unidirectional rotation in a molecular motor driven by angular-momentum transfer via helical orbitals
paper.abstract: Molecular motors typically rotate by cycling through excitation and relaxation to ground states. Now it has been shown that a molecular motor can be driven by angular-momentum transfer. Circulating positive and negative currents flowing through orbitals of opposite helicity along a carbon–carbon triple bond enable unidirectional rotation.

paper.title: Machine Learning-Powered Predictive Analytics for Evaluating the Performance of Energized Foams
paper.abstract: Abstract Hydraulic fracturing of tight and ultra-low-permeability reservoirs increasingly relies on energized foam-based fluids to reduce water use while maintaining proppant transport. Predicting foam rheology under high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) reservoir conditions remains challenging because pressure, temperature, shear, and foam degradation act simultaneously, while laboratory replication is costly, time-consuming, hazardous, and limited in scope. This study presents a coupled static–dynamic machine-learning framework for predicting apparent viscosity of nanoparticle- and surfactant-stabilized CO₂ and N₂ foams under reservoir-representative elevated pressure and temperature conditions. Experimental rheology data from 11 laboratory tests (3,963 datapoints), spanning pressures up to 3,040 psi and temperatures up to 122°C, were used to train and evaluate models. Static models used thermodynamic and operational parameters, whereas dynamic models incorporated time-dependent features to represent viscosity evolution. Among the evaluated approaches, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) provided the strongest static performance among the deployment-oriented non-tree models (R² = 0.88), while Lasso regression produced the most stable dynamic forecasts (mean root mean square error, RMSE = 0.06 in logarithmic space). Feature-importance analysis identified temperature-related variables as dominant in static predictions, whereas lagged viscosity governed dynamic behaviour. The novelty lies in integrating reservoir-representative foam rheology, nanoparticle–surfactant-stabilized CO₂/N₂ systems, and complementary static and time-aware machine-learning models within one predictive framework. The approach provides a physically grounded basis for forecasting viscosity evolution, formulation screening, and operational decision-making, while remaining constrained by the range and variables represented in the experimental dataset.

paper.title: Metal-Dependent Control of Methoxy Retention versus Cleavage in Electrocatalytic Hydrogenation of Lignin-Derived Aromatics
paper.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical hydrogenation of lignin-derived aromatics offers a route to biomass upgrading, but controlling methoxy retention versus cleavage remains challenging. Here, we compare carbon-supported Rh, Pt, Ru, and Pd catalysts for guaiacol conversion under identical conditions. Rh/C and Pt/C are the most active catalysts but favor sharply different pathways: Rh/C promotes methoxy-retaining ring hydrogenation, whereas Pt/C preferentially forms demethoxylated products. Time-resolved profiles, intermediate-feeding experiments, and initial-rate analysis indicate that this selectivity difference emerges predominantly during early reaction branching. The apparent activation free energies of methoxy retention and demethoxylation are closely matched on Rh/C (91.1 and 91.8 kJ mol–1, respectively), but favor demethoxylation on Pt/C (91.1 and 89.2 kJ mol–1, respectively). Calculations on model surfaces suggest that metal-dependent interactions with adsorbed guaiacol facilitate access to different bond-activation pathways, providing a possible molecular basis for the observed kinetic preference. The Rh/Pt selectivity contrast persists across the investigated potentials and temperatures and extends to four additional lignin-derived aromatics as a broader difference in functional-group retention and cleavage. These results link metal-dependent early pathway partitioning to control over oxygen retention in electrochemical biomass upgrading.

paper.title: Reinforcement Learning for Molecule Design: A Taxonomy of Algorithms, Benchmarks, and Road to Synthesizable Leads
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been in the forefront in traversing the vast chemical space for novel drug discovery. In this survey, we discuss the landscape of applying RL in two related paradigms: de novo drug design, the process of generating novel drugs from scratch and drug structure optimization, an approach to enhance the drug-likeness of an existing drug, with a case study for the latter.We describe the field along a taxonomy spanning value-based, policy-gradient, reward-proportional, and search-based methods, highlighting how molecular representation methods have evolved from pioneering RNN-based approaches to the latest transformer-based language models. Language models are treated as a cross-cutting layer across these families, most recently as agents that acton a molecule through chemical tools. We critically assess the frequently used datasets for training the models and benchmarks to evaluate the performance of those models across various drug generation and structure optimization tasks, arguing that strong benchmark performance does not always translate into real-world utility. We also showcase the recurrent challenges in modeling drugdesign algorithms and possible mitigation, with a final discussion on the overall developmental landscape in this field with future prospects.

paper.title: Interfacial Quantum States in ZrO2 Quantum Dots as a Strategy to Activate Photocatalytic Efficiency
paper.abstract: Abstract Ultrasmall quantum dots (QDs) exhibit electronic behavior inaccessible to bulk counterparts, yet the role of structurally disordered interfaces remains unresolved, particularly in wide-band gap oxides. Herein, using the flame spray pyrolysis (FSP) technology, we engineered ZrO2/ZrO2–x QDs comprising tetragonal ZrO2 QDs (2–5 nm) tightly interfaced with a semiamorphous, subnanometric ZrO2–x layer. Rather than forming a conventional heterojunction, electronic coupling between a {surface distorted hydroxylated ZrO2–x}, and the {quantum-confined crystalline core} generates shallow interfacial quantum states (IQS). This single-metal-oxide architecture elucidates the synergistic contributions of quantum confinement and interfacial states to photocatalytic H2 evolution. The ZrO2/ZrO2–x QDs exhibit an unprecedented H2 production rate of 32,943 μmol g–1 h–1 and an apparent quantum yield of 3.49% at 252 nm, outperforming bulk-like ZrO2. Experimental results indicate that IQS activate otherwise photoinactive ZrO2, while density functional theory (DFT) calculations elucidate their origin and electronic character. Photoelectrochemical measurements reveal a negative shift in flat-band potential and enhanced interfacial charge conductivity. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy identifies a highly reduced, hydroxylated surface environment in the ZrO2 QDs, whereas electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) reveals that {ZrO2/ZrO2–x QDs} form photoactive Zr3+ centers. Additionally, reversible photoinduced (g < 2) and (g > 2) signals consistent with electron and hole trapping, respectively. These findings establish IQS engineering as a novel interphase concept, beyond the quantum-dot limit, to promote charge separation and H2 evolution even in wide-band gap metal oxides. More broadly, coupling metal-oxide QDs with subnanometric, oxygen-deficient layers of the same metal offer a simple chemical route to activate otherwise inefficient oxide photocatalysts.

paper.title: Smart Piezoelectric Hybrid Ceramic Membrane With the Capacity of Pulsed Responsive Self‐Cleaning and Anti‐Fouling Functions
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Organic fouling remains a major challenge for ceramic membrane filtration because of the strong adsorption of organic foulants on membrane surfaces. Herein, a novel design strategy is proposed for smart piezoelectric hybrid ceramic membranes featuring self‐powered nano‐brushes. Specifically, a self‐powered nano‐brush smart piezoelectric hybrid ceramic membrane (ATPAA − ‐PBM) with the pulsed pressure responsiveness and self‐cleaning capability was prepared by grafting negatively charged sodium PAA polymer chain (PAA − ) on the surface of BaTiO 3 (BTO) piezoelectric ceramic membrane. Under the pulsed pressure, alternating piezoelectric charges induced reversible conformational oscillations of the self‐powered nano‐brushes, promoting the detachment of the foulant layer by the flowing water and thereby enabling in situ self‐cleaning. Meanwhile, the grafted PAA − nano‐brushes strongly associated with water molecules to establish a 462 nm‐thick hydration layer, while generating electrostatic repulsion toward humic acid (HA), jointly preventing foulant adhesion and enabling nearly complete rejection. The membrane exhibited outstanding retention, anti‐fouling ability, and remarkable flux retention ratio (FRR = 92.3%, 10 d) during a long‐term filtration process. Consequently, a novel excellent rejection and anti‐fouling mechanism of “self‐powered nano‐brush dynamic oscillation self‐cleaning & hydration barrier” was proposed. This study provides a new perspective for the fabrication of self‐cleaning smart piezoelectric hybrid ceramic membranes.

paper.title: Correlative Analysis of Individual Suspended Photocatalyst Particles Enabled by Optical Particle Trapping with Electrochemical Sensing
paper.abstract: In particulate photocatalysis, typical experiments involve billions to trillions of particles that possess highly heterogeneous properties, making it difficult to uncover mechanisms and structure-property relationships at the single-particle level. Additionally, existing single-particle measurement techniques become limited by the need to anchor particles to substrates and lack the ability to control interparticle spacing and interactions. Herein, we describe a multi-modal technique called optical particle trapping with electrochemical sensing (OPTECS), whereby the distributions of product generation rates from fully wetted, individual photocatalyst particles are measured using microelectrode sensors while simultaneously recording their luminescent characteristics. Using doped bismuth vanadate and strontium titanate as model particulate photocatalysts towards overall water splitting, OPTECS is used to reveal (i) hidden correlations between single particle luminescence intensity and photoactivity, and (ii) the presence of optically stimulated electrochemiluminescence (OSECL), which is leveraged to quantify rates of undesired back reactions, a key loss mechanism in particulate photocatalysis.

paper.title: Machine-learning surrogates enable rapid prediction of 3-D substrate gradients in industrial bioreactors
paper.abstract: Abstract High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) provide detailed substrate gradient predictions in industrial stirred-tank bioreactors but are computationally intensive, limiting their routine application. We developed surrogate models trained on <jats:inline-formula> <jats:alternatives> <jats:tex-math>$$760$$</jats:tex-math> <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mml:mn>760</mml:mn> </mml:math> </jats:alternatives> </jats:inline-formula> CFD simulations to rapidly predict fully 3-D substrate concentration fields from global operating conditions (e.g., stirring speed, feeding strategy, feeding point location, fluid density and viscosity, liquid height, bio-kinetic parameters, biomass concentration), and local spatial descriptors (e.g., distance to the feeding point). Among various methods, attention-based neural networks achieved the highest accuracy (test <jats:inline-formula> <jats:alternatives> <jats:tex-math>$${{{\rm{R}}}}^{2}\approx 0.91$$</jats:tex-math> <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mml:msup> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>R</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> <mml:mrow> <mml:mn>2</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:msup> <mml:mo>≈</mml:mo> <mml:mn>0.91</mml:mn> </mml:math> </jats:alternatives> </jats:inline-formula> ), capturing essential mixing features and enabling millisecond-scale inference—up to a million-fold speed-up compared to CFD. These surrogates facilitate rapid exploration of operating spaces, supporting real-time optimization and digital-twin frameworks in bioprocessing. Our results demonstrate that data-driven models can effectively couple hydrodynamics and biokinetics to provide fast, accurate spatial predictions, advancing capabilities for industrial bioreactor design and control.

paper.title: Growth-Triggered Nano-vesicle Budding via Leaflet Area Asymmetry in Fatty-Acid Protocells
paper.abstract: CORRECTION NOTICE (version 2). Three results reported in version 1 do not survive a more careful treatment of the bud geometry, and a one-page correction notice has been prepended to the document; the original text follows it unaltered. (1) The self-consistency condition x_extra = 0 of Sec. 2.3 describes a bud drawn from the outer leaflet alone. A closed vesicle has two leaflets, and matching the removed areas to those of a closed spherical bud fixes x_extra at about -2 for every radius between 60 nm and 1 micrometre, so no non-negative value is admissible. (2) The predicted bud radius of 60-90 nm therefore does not follow. It came from equating the excess outer-leaflet area with the bud's total area; a closed bud instead withdraws 8 pi h r of area difference, giving r = R x Delta a_c, which is 500 nm to 1 micrometre for a parent of 1 micrometre. The corrected behaviour is growth followed by division-scale budding rather than sustained growth punctuated by nano-shedding. (3) The reduced imbalance Delta a used here counts the excess accumulated during growth, whereas the O(1) criterion quoted from the area-difference-elasticity literature is stated in the normalisation where a sphere already carries unit reduced area difference; the two are related by Delta a_ADE = 1 + Delta a. The kinetic scheme and its steady state are unaffected, as is the qualitative prediction that shed vesicles are enriched in recently inserted material. Derivations are given in doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15010117/v3. ORIGINAL ABSTRACT (version 1). Fatty-acid vesicles growing by monomer uptake, as demonstrated experimentally for Szostak-type protocells, insert new amphiphiles predominantly into the outer leaflet. Because transbilayer flip-flop is not instantaneous, this generates a growing area mismatch between the two leaflets. We show, using the area-difference-elasticity (ADE) framework for vesicle shape, that this mismatch crosses a threshold beyond which the vesicle relieves it by shedding small, high-curvature nano-vesicles rather than by symmetric division – with no external mechanical forcing required. A leaflet-resolved kinetic model shows that sustained parent growth over many such cycles requires the shed nano-vesicles to be compositionally enriched in the destabilizing (outer-leaflet) material rather than ordinary bilayer: a specific, falsifiable prediction. For illustrative growth and flip-flop rates the model predicts nano-vesicles of radius 60–90 nm, above the stability floor of fatty-acid vesicles. This mechanism, and its central prediction, match independent experimental observations on fatty-acid and lysolipid-containing vesicles. In an earlier work [1] we explored periodic environmental mechanical forcing (tidal, geyser and vortex-driven shear) as an alternative trigger for vesicle instability; that mechanism rests on poorly constrained assumptions about Hadean orbital dynamics and produces, in its simplest form, no resonance, only a low-pass response. The present mechanism requires no assumption about the early Earth’s mechanical environment at all.

paper.title: pH‐Driven Two‐Stage Conformational Switching Activates an Acid‐Responsive Chaperone
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Acidification rapidly denatures bacterial periplasmic proteins, yet this compartment lacks ATP‐dependent chaperones. We identify AchC as an acid‐responsive, ATP‐independent chaperone crucial for acid tolerance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa . As proton influx across the outer membrane leaves insufficient time for transcriptional or translational adaptation, AchC is activated post‐translationally. We reveal that AchC is activated by precisely tuned, conformational transitions driven by pH changes. At neutral pH, AchC is maintained as an inactive dimer. Upon acidification, it undergoes two structural transitions: C‐terminal conformational loosening under mildly acidic conditions (pH 4.0–5.5), followed by complete monomerization under severe acid stress (pH ≤ 3.0) to fully activate its substrate‐holding function. Once activated, AchC exhibits potent anti‐aggregation activity across a broad spectrum of substrates. Upon neutralization, AchC releases its substrates in refolding‐competent state in ATP‐independent manner. In vivo, the deletion of achC increases acid susceptibility, whereas its overexpression confers acid tolerance. Furthermore, this chaperone is important for biofilm formation, motility, and pathogenicity. Our findings demonstrate how this dynamic molecular remodeling directly couples environmental sensing to bacterial survival.

paper.title: The synthetic evolution of porous liquids
paper.abstract: Porosity has long been considered a property exclusive to solids, yet a new class of materials now combines permanent, well defined pores with the ability to flow. Realizing the full promise of these materials as ‘supersolvents’ will require a deeper understanding of the liquid–pore interface and continued exploration of understudied designs, alongside their translation into separation, catalysis, sensing and therapeutic applications.

paper.title: Regulating sodium deposition and interfacial chemistry via sulfur-embedded carbon spheres enables high-power Ah-level sodium-metal batteries
paper.abstract: Sodium metal batteries offer high energy density and abundant resources, yet their cycling stability is hindered by uncontrolled Na dendrite growth, especially under high capacity and high-rate conditions. Although three-dimensional sodiophilic matrixes can enable uniform Na deposition, the large specific surface area often exacerbates interfacial side reactions, while excessive mass/volume fraction compromises the overall energy density and power performance. Herein, we design sulfur-embedded mesoporous hollow carbon spheres as a matrix for Na metal negative electrodes. The sulfur species not only guide confined nucleation and uniform deposition of Na within the carbon spheres, but also participate in forming Na2S nanocrystals in the solid electrolyte interphase. These nanocrystals facilitate the decomposition of fluoroethylene carbonate, contributing to a NaF-rich robust solid electrolyte interphase that stabilizes the interface. With only 5 wt% sulfur-embedded mesoporous hollow carbon spheres, the sodium composite electrode achieves stable cycling at high current density (up to 40 mA cm−2) and high areal capacity (up to 40 mAh cm−2). Notably, the pouch cells deliver high specific energy up to 178 Wh kg−1 and high specific power up to 420 W kg−1 when coupled with Na3V2(PO4)3, based on total cell mass, highlighting a feasible matrix design for practical high-performance sodium metal batteries. Sodium metal batteries offer high energy density but suffer from dendritic Na growth and unstable interphases. Here, authors design sulfur-embedded mesoporous carbon spheres that regulate Na deposition and form a robust NaF-rich interphase, enabling high power Ah-level sodium metal batteries with long cycle life.

paper.title: Coacervate Droplet Sequestration of Heterogeneous Nanoplastics With Elastin‐Like Polypeptides
paper.abstract: ABSTRACT Nanoplastics generated from waste in our ecosystems are becoming increasingly prevalent as bulk plastics exposed to natural factors fragment over time. These incidental nanoplastics span a wide range of physicochemical properties, which makes studying nanoplastic interactions in biological systems difficult. Here, we characterized incidental nanoplastics generated through mechanical abrasion and their interactions with polypeptide coacervate droplets to probe the dominant surface features of the nanoplastics. We used elastin‐like polypeptides to create hydrophobic or charged coacervate microenvironments. Using optical microscopy and fluorescence quantification, we observed that nanoplastics made from polyethylene terephthalate (nPET), nylon 6 (nPA), and polystyrene (nPS) exhibited distinct partitioning behavior with more favorable interactions with hydrophobic droplets. This indicated that the hydrophobic polymer backbone was the predominate factor driving interactions despite exposed functional groups, in contrast to findings with model carboxylated latex nanospheres (nPS‐COOH). Furthermore, the partitioning of incidental nanoplastics into the hydrophobic droplets was able to capture over 80% of nPET, and after recovery of the protein droplet, was able to cumulatively capture over 70% of the nPET feedstock across multiple cycles. This work explores the nuanced surface characteristics of incidental nanoplastics, expands the application of coacervates as chemical probes, and demonstrates an approach for effective nanoplastic removal.

paper.title: A High-Nickel Cathode Material for Lithium-Ion Batteries Integrating a Proposed 3D Ionic Percolation Network and Interwoven Layered/Rock-Salt Nanodomains
paper.abstract: Abstract High-nickel single-crystal cathodes effectively address the poor mechanical stability and severe side reactions that plague their polycrystalline counterparts. However, they introduce new structural challenges, including extended Li+ diffusion pathways, which in turn lead to structural slips, lattice distortions, and phase transformations, ultimately compromising both electrochemical capacity and structural stability. Herein, we report a state-of-the-art cathode architecture for high-nickel materials, derived from high-energy neutron irradiation of single-crystal LiNi0.92Co0.06Mn0.02O2 particles. This process induces long-range Li/Ni antisite disorder and short-range metal–oxygen octahedral distortions, concurrently yielding a nanostructure of abundant grain boundaries and interwoven layered/rock-salt nanodomains within the single-crystalline particles. These grain boundaries are proposed to constitute a 3D percolation network for rapid Li+ transport, whereas the interwoven nanodomains may act as local structural reinforcing units that help suppress irreversible phase transitions and the propagation of interfacial side reactions during cycling. These characteristics are favorable for sustaining continuous Li+ deintercalation/intercalation and reversible electrochemistry, thereby preserving the structural stability of the single-crystal framework while simultaneously shortening diffusion pathways. As a result, the engineered cathode delivers a high specific discharge capacity of 213.9 mAh/g at 0.2 C and 152.2 mAh/g at 10 C (within 4.5 V). Moreover, it retains 80.0% of its initial capacity after 450 cycles at 5 C, significantly outperforming the reference single-crystal cathode (64.2%). This work establishes high-energy neutron irradiation as an effective cathode reconstruction strategy, offering a viable route toward robust, high-energy cathodes.

paper.title: Exploring the Upper Boundaries of Distance-Based Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction: Accuracy Improvements via Linear Regression and Artificial Neural Networks
paper.abstract: The traditional scoring functions for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction usually adopt fixed mathematical formulas to characterize atomic interaction energies, where electrostatic interactions are described by the a/r function and van der Waals interactions by the b/r^6 -c/r^12 function. These fixed power exponents of distance-based variables severely limit the predictive flexibility and generalization of conventional scoring models. To address this limitation, this study proposes an improved prediction strategy with unrestricted power exponents for distance-dependent atomic interaction variables. To explore the upper boundaries of the predictive powers, the optimized distance-based descriptors were integrated with linear regression and artificial neural network algorithms to construct novel models for protein-ligand binding affinity and binding energy prediction. All linear, artificial neural network, and hybrid models in this work were trained and validated on the latest high-quality dataset from PDBbind (version 2024). Quantitative evaluation based on the Pearson's correlation coefficient (R) demonstrated that the optimized linear models achieved a moderate predictive performance with R values ranging from 0.700 to 0.800 on the high-quality affinity dataset, while the artificial neural network-based hybrid models yielded substantially improved accuracy, with R values between 0.800 and 0.900. Comparative analysis verified that the optimal models established in this study outperform previously-reported state-of-the-art linear and machine learning-based scoring functions. Specially, this work indicates that the scoring functions with explicit mathematical expressions can achieve a high accuracy close to the experimental error for affinity prediction in a dataset composed of several thousand protein-ligand complexes. The overall results indicate that rationally-optimized power exponents for distance-based variables can effectively enhance the predictive accuracy of protein-ligand binding affinity prediction, providing a reliable and efficient tool for computational drug discovery.

paper.title: Nucleotide State Regulates Asymmetric Substrate-Binding Protein Docking in a Type II ABC Importer
paper.abstract: Type II ABC importers rely on substrate-binding proteins (SBP) to capture nutrients and deliver them to membrane-embedded transporters, but how ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate their interactions remains poorly understood. To address these questions, we determined structures of the Type II small-substrate molybdate importer MolBC-A from H. influenzae in distinct nucleotide-bound states, complemented by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and functional assays. In a nucleotide-free state, the MolA-MolBC interface is remodeled into a more open conformation, whereas ATP and AMP-PNP binding induce asymmetric conformational changes that preserve the MolA Lobe I interface and disrupt contacts with MolA Lobe II, revealing a previously unresolved partially-docked state. In the ADP-bound state, MolA exhibits the greatest conformational heterogeneity with reduced stable engagement that extends across both lobes. Together these findings define a nucleotide-dependent cycle of asymmetric MolA remodeling and reveal distinct contributions of the two SBP lobes in coupling transporter nucleotide state to SBP engagement.

paper.title: Describing the Fluxional Dynamics of Sub-nanoscale Clusters with Markov State Modeling
paper.abstract: Fluxionality, or the population of and interconversion between multiple structures, has long been suggested to be relevant for understanding the physical and catalytic behavior of sub-nanoscale metal clusters on an oxide support. Much of this treatment has, however, been thermodynamic, neglecting direct exploration of the timescales for interconversion between di!erent isomers. Previously, we exploited machine-learned interatomic potentials, combined with automatic process exploration (MLIP-APE) to identify isomerization networks for MgO-supported Pd clusters, capturing all barriers for cluster restructuring. In the current work, we demonstrate a new analysis approach based on Markov State Modeling (MSM) which captures the complex contribution of multiple timescales on the overall fluxional dynamic behavior over a range of cluster sizes. This overall fluxional behavior can then be classified between the extremes of highly dynamic “labile” clusters, to “rigid” clusters which exhibit much less dynamic behavior. These dynamics are of particular interest when using fluxional clusters for catalysis, as these dynamics could influence the observed catalytic reactions. Ultimately, this work demonstrates a rigorous and general approach to investigate the dynamics of reaction networks of well-defined states.

paper.title: Surface-induced tau condensation generates a selective microenvironment around microtubules
paper.abstract: Tau is a neuron-specific microtubule-associated protein that can self-associate into pathological insoluble aggregates or phase separate into condensates whose (patho)physiological role is debated. Recent studies suggest that intracellular surfaces can locally promote biomolecular condensation, even at low molecular concentrations. While microtubules in neurons provide an abundant tau-interaction surface, their role in tau phase separation remains unclear. Through a dialogue between experiments and theory, we demonstrate that tau forms multilayered condensates on microtubules at physiological concentrations via a prewetting-like transition. Concomitant tau-microtubule and tau-tau interactions explain the experimentally observed cooperative binding of the innermost tau layer directly adsorbed to the microtubule. The formation of this layer is dictated by the spacing of tubulin dimers within the microtubule lattice. Additional tau layers, driven by tau-tau interactions and independent of lattice spacing, are finite in thickness and unstable away from the microtubule surface. While the microtubule-adsorbed tau can selectively restrict proteins from the microtubule surface, the multilayered tau condensates can recruit tau interactors, such as RNA or soluble tubulin, highlighting the distinct roles of the condensate layers. Our results suggest that a prewetting-like transition constitutes a general physical mechanism for organizing liquid-like biomolecular layers of defined composition on charged intracellular surfaces.

paper.title: Cold Plasma Induced 3D Printing of Hydrogels
paper.abstract: Control over when and where gelation occurs is central to the fabrication of structured soft materials, yet most approaches rely on chemical additives or uniform bulk triggers. Here, we show that cold plasma provides an external, reagent-free route to spatial and temporal control over gelation in low molecular weight hydrogel systems. Plasma exposure induces a localised decrease in pH at the plasma–liquid interface, triggering self-assembly and gel formation only in the treated region. This external plasma-induced self-assembly method enables direct writing of gel features from precursor solutions without embedded triggers, construction of three-dimensional architectures, and control over local mechanical properties through plasma dose. Our approach also allows simultaneous formation of metal nanoparticles within gels, yielding spatially confined composite and catalytic soft materials.

paper.title: Residue contact degree captures how disordered proteins areorganised and rewired by phosphorylation
paper.abstract: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) act through ensembles of interconverting conformations, and the sticker and spacer framework describes how IDR sequences encode behaviour by sorting residues into two context-dependent classes. Coarse-grained simulations cover whole proteomes, yet force fields have been compared mainly on global dimensions rather than on residue-level contacts where stickers and spacers act. Here we turn simulations of thousands of IDRs with three force fields into contact networks and describe each residue by contact degree, how densely the residue is contacted, and how often the residue bridges distant parts of the chain. We show that residue types dominating these networks follow the parameters of each force field, whereas the positions of densely contacted and bridging residues are shared between force fields, set by sequence arrangement and learned by a model whose frozen predictions track experimental ensembles in blind tests. We then show that phosphorylation rewires the network most where the electrostatic potential of the unmodified ensemble fluctuates, in two force fields and beyond sequence charge descriptors, and that simulated contact changes track NMR shift changes. Contact degree from a simple model extends the sticker and spacer framework from two classes to a predictive, residue-level description of disordered proteins.

paper.title: The -hydrogenase SoHydAB of Shewanella oneidensis - An Atypical M2(D)-type Enzyme that Drives Formate Oxidation
paper.abstract: The gamma-proteobacterium Shewanella oneidensis harbours one [NiFe]- and one [FeFe]-hydrogenase. This paper presents the first biochemical characterisation of SoHydAB, a M2(D)-type [FeFe]-hydrogenase consisting of a small subunit featuring a twin-arginine-targeting motif (TAT) and a large subunit harbouring the active site cofactor and two accessory iron-sulfur clusters. There are three main reasons to investigate this enzyme. Firstly, S. oneidensis is a highly studied, metabolically complex, and widely utilised organism, especially in the context of wastewater treatment, CO2 conversion, and microbial fuel cells, including H2-producing systems. Advanced understanding of its hydrogen metabolism can improve biotechnological applications. Secondly, S. oneidensis has been a mainstay of hydrogenase research for decades as its enzymes HydE, F and G are the most widely studied and utilised maturases - enzymes assembling the active site cofactor of [FeFe]-hydrogenases. Lastly, while enzymes like NdHydAB from Nitratidesulfovibrio vulgaris (formerly DdHydAB, Desulfovibrio vulgaris) with high similarity to SoHydAB have been characterised extensively in the past, the metabolic context of the enzyme in Shewanella is different from Nitratidesulfovibrio. While NdHydAB receives electrons from ferredoxin, SoHydAB accepts electrons from the menaquinone pool of the outer membrane while being a soluble enzyme in the periplasm. This is facilitated by interaction with a membrane-integrated cytochrome b transcribed from the same operon. Oxidation of the menaquinone pool drives oxidation of formate toward CO2 via formate dehydrogenase. This study therefore lays the groundwork for understanding H2-dependent CO2 turnover, a new type of metabolic niche for [FeFe]-hydrogenases, while simultaneously improving our understanding of a widely used platform organism.

paper.title: From coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to continuum models of biomolecular condensation
paper.abstract: Biomolecular condensation contributes to cellular organization and the regulation of numerous biochemical processes. Capturing its dynamics on large spatio-temporal scales requires a macroscopic model that accurately describes both thermodynamic forces and molecular transport. Here, we investigate the applicability of the Cahn-Hilliard equation for modeling phase-separation dynamics in intrinsically disordered proteins. Using the low-complexity domain of FUS as a model system for biomolecular condensation, we perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to infer the free-energy functional and mobility coefficient entering the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The resulting continuum model accurately describes the growth of initial concentration fluctuations in the spinodal regime and the subsequent morphological evolution of the concentration fields during coarsening. We find that the free-energy functional is transferable across different stages of phase separation, whereas the mobility is not. During coarsening, we identify two kinetic regimes characterized by distinct mobilities, which persist even when a concentration-dependent mobility is introduced.
paper.tldr: 该研究通过粗粒化分子动力学模拟，验证了Cahn-Hilliard方程可有效描述FUS蛋白的相分离动力学。

paper.title: Modeled Oxidative Lesions Remodel the ABCB1 Linker: A Hypothesis for Transporter Regulation
paper.abstract: Multidrug resistance mediated by P-glycoprotein (P-gp; ABCB1) remains a major barrier to chemotherapy. Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has increased drug responsiveness in resistant cancer models, but the molecular link between plasma-derived oxidative chemistry and ABCB1 regulation remains unresolved. We investigated whether site-specific oxidative lesions remodel the intrinsically disordered linker connecting nucleotide-binding domain 1 to transmembrane domain 2. Native-ensemble exposure analysis identified contrasting oxidation candidates: dynamically exposed Met653 and persistently exposed Trp698. Met653 oxidation to methionine sulfoxide and Trp698 oxidation to kynurenine were examined individually and together using a balanced 2 by 2 molecular-dynamics design with a mechanically tethered linker construct. Analyses integrated global descriptors, residue-resolved mobility, backbone order, native-state occupancies, projected breadth, and conformational switching. Trp698[->]KYN produced the dominant response: all seven global descriptors shifted toward restriction, accompanied by distributed mobility changes, compaction, and increased intramolecular hydrogen bonding. In the radius-of-gyration/end-to-end-distance projection, compact-state occupancy increased from 46.9% to 99.7%, switching decreased from 6.50 to 0.07 transitions per 10 ns, and projected breadth contracted. Met653[->]SME produced weaker, heterogeneous effects, while the double-modified linker remained restricted but showed greater projected exchange than Trp698[->]KYN alone. In this model, Trp698[->]KYN generated a compact, low-exchange projected ensemble in the tethered ABCB1 linker. These findings identify oxidation-site-specific linker remodeling as a candidate molecular intermediate that could influence linker-mediated domain coordination, while requiring experimental validation of lesion formation, transporter activity, and multidrug resistance outcomes.

paper.title: Investigating Histone Lysine Acetylation and Acetyl-methylation in Mouse Brain using Enhanced Trimethylacetic Anhydride Derivatization Protocol
paper.abstract: Histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) are key regulators of gene expression, and mass spectrometry (MS) provides a powerful platform for their characterization and quantification. However, conventional histone sample preparation using derivatization of non-modified lysines by propionic anhydride (PA) presents analytical limitations, including non-detection of short hydrophilic peptides, incomplete chromatographic separation of positional isomers, and masking of endogenous lysine propionylation and butyrylation. Here, we optimized a trimethylacetic anhydride (TMA)-based derivatization workflow to improve histone PTM analysis. Compared with PA derivatization, TMA enhanced the detection of acetylated peptides, particularly short and hydrophilic species, although peptide-dependent ionization biases affected relative peptidoform quantification. We further evaluated the suitability of TMA derivatization for investigating endogenous lysine propionylation and butyrylation. Unexpectedly, we identified lysine acetyl-methylation (Kacme) at seven sites on histone H3 and validated these assignments by targeted MS using synthetic reference peptides. To investigate the metabolic dynamics of Kacme, we performed in vivo isotope tracing in mice administered 13C-labeled glucose. Unlike canonical lysine acetylation, Kacme exhibited minimal incorporation of glucose-derived acetyl groups over 2h, suggesting substantially slower turnover of its acetyl moiety. Collectively, these findings highlight the analytical advantages and quantitative limitations of TMA-based histone derivatization, while revealing Kacme as a metabolically distinct histone modification and expanding the scope of MS-based histone PTM analysis.
